en: [The *Dvaitadyumaṇipariśiṣṭa*: An objection: Surely, it is intended by this text that the distinction between the Supreme [Goal] and [ordinary] goals is established precisely through the difference between the cessation of suffering and the attainment of pleasure. Therefore, an explanation that supplements this by including a distinction among desired goals (*iṣṭasādhana*) is improper. If you say this, we reply: No, because the status of being a human goal (*puruṣārthatā*) was previously stated solely on the basis of having "mere desire" (*iṣṭamātra*) as its object; thus, the "Supreme Goal" (*parameṣṭa*) was not even under consideration there. Nor can it be argued that even in that context, the status of being the ultimate fruit was stated solely on the basis of having the Supreme Goal as its object. For if that were so, it would contradict the introductory statement: "For whatever is desired by someone... (*yaddhi yasyeṣṭam*).

Furthermore, even there, the term "supreme" (*parameṣṭa*) does not denote the ultimate goal itself; for if it did, it would have been stated that "whatever is someone's supreme [goal], that alone should be taught to them, and nothing else. Since it is precisely the worldly way of life that is now being propounded, and since for worldly people the attainment of pleasure and the cessation of pain are indeed their supreme goals, it follows that only those two—pleasure and the cessation of pain—should be taught by such statements as "pleasure is [the goal]" and "the cessation of pain is [the goal]," and only such a statement would be worthy of acceptance.

But this does not apply to Vedic or worldly sentences such as "one should sacrifice" or "one should cook," which communicate a desired end that serves as the means [to that goal]; for those have as their object a supreme desired end, and no one indeed accepts [them] in that manner [as mere instrumental ends].

But is it not the case that even the "means to the desired" (*iṣṭasādhana*) is included there by way of implication? And thus the meaning is: "For whatever is someone's supreme desire, whether directly or through a succession, one or the other of those two [the desire or its means] must be understood; nothing else. Nor should it be asked why only the "desired" (*iṣṭa*) is mentioned later on. Between the two, in the present context, it was stated that "the Lord of Ramā is the desired" in order to declare the suitability of the statement revealing the Lord as being acceptable for some people at least, by virtue of its being a revealer of what is desired.

The meaning is simply "the supreme desired object. Even so, one might ask how the sentence can be effective since it does not produce activity or other such results; to resolve this objection, the phrase "of the experience of the desired object" is stated.

Some explain this statement as follows: here, by the term "experience" (*anubhava*), merely a cognition regarding a present, desired object related to oneself is intended. By this term, if one intends a cognition other than memory, there is no room for the objection that the knowledge produced by the sentence "That which is not mixed with suffering," etc., would also result in being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, if one intends direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), there is no room for the objection that the Lord's understanding generated by the Veda would fail to be a human goal because it lacks the nature of direct perception. Thus, these criticisms find no footing.

In this regard, the following is considered: even so, at the time when pleasure produced by eating and such is arising for Caitra, and during the state of the absence of suffering, there arises—due to a statement uttered by Maitra, namely, "O Caitra, pleasure exists in you; an absence of suffering exists in you now"—a cognition residing in Caitra. This would result in that cognition being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) with respect to Caitra. And this is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

For if such a statement were uttered by Maitra, there would arise in people the cognition, "This person fulfills my desired end," just as they have toward one who performs other benefits, and the cognition, "And this Caitra is a benefactor. But that is not the case; on the contrary, people become mockers, saying, "What is there for you to say? It is already happening!"

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "related to oneself" (*svasambandhī*), if "relation" (*sambandha*) is introduced as the defining characteristic of the relation itself, then because another's pleasure stands in some kind of indirect relation (*paramparāsambandha*) to oneself, a cognition whose object is another's pleasure and so forth would also result in being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). It might be argued that "another's pleasure is not desired by oneself. If that were the case, then the term "related to oneself" would be rendered redundant for the purpose of excluding such [cognitions].

Furthermore, since the absolute absence of a particular suffering exists both in oneself and in others as a single entity, the experience of the absence of suffering residing in Caitra would result in being a human goal (puruṣārtha) for Maitra as well. Even if "residing in oneself" were included in the definition of knowledge, then a verbal cognition regarding the aforementioned absence of suffering residing in Caitra that resides in Maitra would likewise [erroneously] qualify as such. If, on the other hand, one specifies "inherence in oneself" or "ownership by oneself," then the direct perception (sākṣātkāra) of the absence of suffering would not be included.

This is because the absence of suffering is neither inherent in oneself nor owned by oneself; for in the final system (siddhānta), there is no such thing as inherence (samavāya). Even if one were to avoid the aforementioned fault by defining "inherence" merely as a form of occurrence (vṛttitva), there would still be a failure to include the direct perception of pleasure (sukha-sākṣātkāra) according to the literal definition and its refined interpretation, since pleasure and the like are attributes of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Furthermore, in the view that [the absence of suffering] must be owned by oneself, the knowledge of the Lord (īśvara-jñāna) would not be included, as it is not owned by anyone other than Himself.

In reality, the term "desired" (*iṣṭa*) in the phrase "experience of the desired" (*iṣṭānubhava*) refers exclusively to the Supreme Desired (*parameṣṭa*). The particle "only" (*eva*) indicates that it is not qualified by attributes such as being a generator of activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth. The term "experience" (*anubhava*) refers exclusively to knowledge (*jñāna*).

Since it serves the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) and is the supreme fruit (*paramaphala*), and because there is no impossibility regarding the fact that even a certain supreme knowledge—which does not produce activity and so forth—is observed to have the nature of a fruit, and since the statement "the experience of God is also of the nature of a fruit" has been introduced, there is no room for the charge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as the verbal cognition of pleasure and so forth; for if one assumes the purport of this sentence to lie in the rule that such knowledge in general is of the nature of a fruit, there is no basis [for such an objection]. The two sentences beginning with "na hi" are the justification for that very point.

Furthermore, since it is the supreme good (*parameṣṭa*) itself that has been introduced as the subject, its status as the supreme good is here implied by its not being of the nature of either pleasure or pain.

One might object: "Having established the status of the supreme good intended by the author of the root-text (*mūlakṛt*) with the words 'Not [pleasure]' and so forth, he will subsequently establish the authority of the Veda for those of intermediate devotion through its being a means to the desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), etc.; thus, for the sake of consistency between the preceding and following sections, why resort to an interpretation of the word *iṣṭa* as referring to the general category of the desired, thereby involving a forced supplementation (*pūraṇa*)? We reply: No, because even in your own interpretation, the supplementation of "being a means to the desired" is already necessitated.

However, it is more appropriate that the word "desired" (*iṣṭa*), occurring within a sentence containing multiple words, should possess a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇikatva*) toward the supreme good (*parameṣṭa*). Furthermore, it is altogether improper to claim that the supreme good is to be conveyed by the sentence as being on the same footing as the means to the desired end; for in common worldly usage, questions and answers are observed only regarding the means to one's own happiness and the like, as we never see a question such as "What is my happiness like? followed by an answer such as "Your happiness is like this."

Furthermore, the statement that the direct perception of pleasure (*sukha-sākṣātkāra*) constitutes the nature of the fruit is irrelevant for the purpose of establishing—through subsequent statements such as "of the experience of the desired" (*iṣṭānubhavasya*) and so forth—that the verbal cognition of God (*īśvara-śābda*) is itself the nature of the fruit.

Since the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the perception of indifferent objects such as grass and so forth is established for all, validity therein consists merely in the capacity to convey an object as it actually exists; however, because verbal testimony is for the sake of another, its validity is constituted by its being fruitful. Thus, since the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) proceeds on the basis of this distinction from perception—wherein the direct experience of pleasure is itself the fruit—it follows that the verbal testimony concerning God cannot be established as having the nature of a fruit.

If [the status of being a result] were based merely on the commonality of being a desired cognition, then the cognition of pleasure would also have that status; furthermore, by the commonality of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), even a jar or similar entity would possess it. If the direct perception of pleasure and the verbal cognition [of it] are distinguished as result and non-result solely by virtue of their being direct perception and verbal cognition respectively, then why would the verbal cognition of God not also be non-resultant?

Since the opponent has accepted the rule that there is an absence of being an object of desire for the general class of cognitions that do not produce activity and so forth—on the grounds that perception and other such cognitions which do not produce activity lack the status of being objects of desire—it is appropriate to point out an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in specific cases of perception and the like; thus, there is no inconsistency in our explanation of this statement. Furthermore, the fact that the cognition of God is the ultimate fruit [of inquiry] is established by the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes His being the supreme goal.

Furthermore, in your interpretation, the word *iṣṭa* (desired) found in the root text refers only to the supreme desired object. Consequently, since the meaningfulness of the Veda with respect to intermediate devotees (*madhyama-bhaktas*) is not mentioned, a deficiency in the root text would result. Therefore, an interpretation supplemented by such an addition is indeed appropriate; however, the word *iṣṭa* refers to the desired object in its general sense.

Now, if one does not accept that doubt (*vimati*) is the delimitor of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), then the use of the word "disputed" (*vimata*)—abandoning the specification of the subject such as "the root is liberated" (*mūle mukta*)—would be purposeless. Nor is it correct to say that this is for the sake of making known the necessity of a statement of doubt in all cases; for the Nyāyāmṛta has already refuted the necessity of such a statement by demonstrating that doubt regarding a contradictory probandum is not of the nature of subjecthood (*pakṣatā*). Therefore, that [position] cannot be the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

As for the claim that "disagreement (*vipratipatti*) is indeed necessary; because through disagreement there arises doubt, and through the desire for its result—which is the absence of that [doubt]—there occurs the occasion for inquiry in the form of a formal argument (*nyāyavākya*); thus, disagreement is a constituent part of inquiry": [we reply: But surely, since the two disputants necessarily possess certainty regarding their respective positions, and since the neutral observer and others are likewise learned, where could doubt possibly arise?

Furthermore, if it is argued that a neutral person (*madhyastha*) might employ the statement of conflicting views (*vipratipatti-vākya*) with the thought: "If the fool deliberates or restrains himself, his own reputation will suffer; therefore, to avoid this, the neutral person must examine whether both possess equal learning. Since he has already ascertained one of the two positions based on that examination, there is not even the possibility of doubt—how then could a doubt arise?"—this is not correct.

Even though at that time there is no actual doubt present, it is accepted that the *vipratipatti* (doctrinal dispute) serves as a constituent part of the inquiry (*vicāra*). This is because, although the *vipratipatti* possesses the causal capacity for doubt by virtue of its nature as being "suitable" for doubt, when the cognition of one related term in the form of the *vipratipatti* occurs, there arises a recollection of the other related term in the form of doubt; subsequently, following the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), there arises the cognition of its absence, which is the result. Thus, through the desire for that [result] and the subsequent engagement in the inquiry that brings it about, the *vipratipatti* is intended to be a limb of the inquiry.

Nor should it be argued that since the absence of doubt exists at that time, how could there be a desire for it; for even at a later time, the absence of doubt may persist due to the fear that it might be interrupted by distraction or other factors. Thus, with the thought "May the absence of doubt continue even at a later time," a desire for the inquiry—which serves to maintain that state through means such as strengthening the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) dependent on the experience produced by oneself—is possible.

Nor should it be argued that, in a formal debate (*vāda*) whose sole fruit is the determination of truth, disagreement (*vipratipatti*) is unnecessary—since this is indeed established by the Naiyāyikas and others through the consensus of texts such as the *Pratyakṣāloka*—because in a contentious debate (*jalpa*), since engagement in inquiry is possible solely for the sake of one's own victory, there is no requirement to seek any other fruit. Even so, it must be admitted that without the members of the assembly (*sabhyas*), the presiding judge (*sabhāpati*), and others seeking their own respective fruits, it would be impossible for them to direct their minds toward the debate; therefore, according to the aforementioned reasoning, disagreement serves that purpose [of engaging the audience].

Nor should it be argued that, according to the manner previously stated, there is no intrinsic capacity (*svarūpayogyatā*) for producing a result anywhere because of the absence of a means of proof (*kalpaka*); for since there is no rule that all members of an assembly must be learned, and since doubt regarding such a statement might arise in others through its occurrence outside the assembly, the non-production of a result remains unestablished.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, a sentence that produces ignorance and so forth—which would be the counter-positive (*pratiyogi*) of the fruit consisting in the cessation of ignorance and error—would also necessarily be required. For since ignorance is beginningless (*anādi*), no sentence that could produce it can be established. Furthermore, because the cessation of doubt is rooted in the cessation of ignorance, it does not require a separate effort. Moreover, since there is no rule that all [people] must be settled in a single view, and since there is no single alternative (*koṭi*) to be negated by everyone, it is impossible to point out a sentence of error in the form "this is exactly thus."

Furthermore, the purpose of the *vipratipatti* (statement of conflicting views) is not limited to this alone; another purpose also exists. When the statement of conflicting views is employed, since both alternatives (*koṭi*) have been heard by everyone, it is impossible for either of the two disputants to establish their own victory by first denying those [alternatives] and then apprehending a different subject. Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of an absence of any settled rule regarding victory and defeat.

Thus, when a neutral person himself offers one argument for each side, or when a proponent is unable to support either side, he would be treated as having partiality toward one side or as harboring envy and the like toward himself.

Therefore, since people might suspect that after hearing both sides of a proposition through a statement of disagreement (*vipratipatti*), the two disputants themselves are unable to support the alternative position once they have chosen their own specific thesis, the two disputants—intending to show that no such fault attaches to themselves if they act accordingly immediately after stating, "You yourself must propose some thesis"—must present the *vipratipatti*. For this dual purpose, the *vipratipatti* is indispensable. By this, the objection regarding the offering of counter-arguments based on common characteristics (*sādhāraṇadharma*) and so forth is refuted.

Therefore, in order to fulfill one's own duty, a counter-argument must indeed be presented, just as in the case of the binding of a convention; for there is no insistence on [the necessity of] ultimate constituents.

That is not so; for a statement made by a neutral person—either in Sanskrit in the form: "Sound is the object of the Naiyāyikas' acceptance as a quality (*guṇa*), but of the Mīmāṃsakas' as a substance (*dravya*); therefore, one may adopt whichever position one pleases," or in an equivalent vernacular sentence—suffices to fulfill all the aforementioned purposes. Consequently, there is no necessity for a specific type of *vipratipatti* (contradictory disagreement) consisting of various artificial constructions, such as the capacity to generate verbal cognitions of two contradictory alternatives regarding a single substratum (*dharmin*).

This [objection] cannot be avoided even by the hundreds of arguments stated in the *Nyāyāmṛta*; for in the *Nyāyāmṛta*, it was not said that [the use of the vernacular] is entirely useless, but merely that it is unnecessary. Indeed, there is no obstacle whatsoever to using the vernacular in discourse prior to a formal debate with neutral parties and others; on the contrary, it is precisely that which is appropriate for easy understanding even by common people and the like.

Furthermore, after the proponent and the opponent have been made to adopt their respective positions and so forth in the manner described by another person prompted by the presiding officer (*sabhāpati*), the neutral arbiter (*madhyastha*) is subsequently appointed. In that regard, there is no room for the neutral arbiter to exhibit disagreement; for in all matters, since there is no rule requiring the utterance at any other time of a statement formulated by the neutral arbiter at that moment, doubt is not produced, and because there is no basis for postulating a capacity for such [disagreement] in his essential nature.

Furthermore, even if that [doubt] exists in someone, since knowledge alone does not necessarily produce it in everyone through its own application, it is unfit to be a reminder of doubt for all. Even if it were possible for some, because the future deliberation—which is required to bring about the cessation of doubt—is not present, the mental attention of the assembly president and others cannot be accomplished by it.

For where there is a determination of one side by the presiding officer (*sabhāpati*) and others, our application of attention (*praṇidhāna*) is justified solely for the sake of knowing that excellence which is useful for the honor due to our own duty. Furthermore, when the authority of the two disputants is ascertained, there is no need to make a formal agreement (*samayaviśeṣabandha*), just as there is no need to employ an example in a logical argument (*nyāya*) where the lack of proof is already established; moreover, such an agreement is not accepted as being universally applicable by rule.

Since even a specific statement may serve as a means to establish ignorance in a general sense of security, it is indeed appropriate to point out its application merely for the sake of recalling the result; therefore, one must abandon the insistence on the necessity [of the opponent's position] even regarding the dispute over the members of the syllogism, just as in the case of the members themselves. Now, an objection: since difference also exists in the Consciousness that is the substrate of all—whether that Consciousness be qualified by some attribute or merely indicated by it—is it not impossible, according to my view, for there to be a dispute regarding the alternative of difference with respect to that which is qualified or indicated by the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*)?

Furthermore, in your view, since the difference established by the cognition "the jar is not consciousness" is superimposed upon the consciousness delimited by the jar, you must assert that even though that difference exists in consciousness through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), the cognition "consciousness is not consciousness" is prevented because "in a cognition where the negative particle (*nañ*) is expressed, the relation of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) appears; however, that difference does not exist in consciousness by means of that [qualifier] relation. And thus, although other differences also exist in consciousness through the relation of identity, they do not subsist there by means of the relation of being a qualifier.

And in the present context, a dispute concerning the alternative of difference characterized by the relation of inherence with that [consciousness] which is qualified by liberation is appropriate. Although it may appear at first glance that the difference established by the cognition "consciousness is not a jar" exists in pure consciousness through the relation of qualification (*viśeṣaṇatā*), nevertheless, it exists only in [consciousness] as conditioned by its own adjuncts; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the loss of its purity.

The same applies to other distinctions as well. Since a distinction is unestablished in pure consciousness, and since there is the possibility of a dispute regarding a distinction within consciousness characterized by liberation, one might ask: "How can there be room for the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) when proving [distinction] therein? It must be said that if the inference, or the proposition constituting the point of dispute, apprehends the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) by way of the property consisting of liberation (*muktatva*), then because only that which is qualified by liberation appears in the inference, a distinction is not established in pure consciousness.

Furthermore, since the difference conditioned by that [attribute] is accepted through the sentence that constitutes the counter-argument (*vipratipatti*), it is impossible to establish a position consisting of its negation. Moreover, if it is accepted that an attribute serving as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) sometimes indicates another attribute and sometimes indicates the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself, the following is the resulting conclusion: in certain cases, while not appearing in the resultant cognition itself, it serves to bring about the presence of another attribute that does appear in that resultant cognition.

And in some cases, when the realization has already become the fruit, that which presents only the manifest essential nature while itself not appearing therein is called an "upalakṣaṇa" (indirect indicator) of the essential nature. Examples of this and so forth are clear in the original treatises (*ākara*). Likewise, here too, if [the term] were to present liberation as a distinct attribute (*dharmāntara*) and then itself cease, then the sentence expressing the contradiction would effect a negation of difference in consciousness qualified by that distinct attribute; and that is untenable.

For just as difference is admitted in that which is qualified by liberation, so too is difference admitted in that which is qualified by other attributes. In this way, the proposition would have an established meaning (*siddhārtha*), because difference is accepted in that which is qualified by other attributes. Furthermore, if the definition were merely of the essential nature (*svarūpa-mātra*), then the sentence "the liberated one is not different," or the aforementioned sentence containing a negative particle, would produce a cognition either grasping the mere essential nature—namely, in the form "he possesses the absence of difference" or "he possesses difference."

And likewise, how could those two sentences be sentences of contradiction? For there is an absence of their being generators [of doubt], since the cognition produced by both of them—or any other cognition dependent upon them—is not of the nature of doubt; moreover, there is no doubt whose delimiting property of the subject (dharmitāvacchedaka) is absent. Furthermore, how could even an inference apprehend consciousness as characterized by the aforementioned state of being unspoken? For that [inference] lacks the absence of a delimiting property of the subject and so forth.

Now, you might think: "The manifestation [of difference] as characterized by liberation means that difference appears merely as being co-referential with liberation in its aspect as a qualifier (*prakāra*). However, the manifestation of the relation to the qualifier as being delimited by liberation is the manifestation of it as qualified by that [liberation]. And since in the present case you accept that difference exists only in consciousness (*cit*) as qualified by something [else], a dispute regarding the non-existence of difference in pure consciousness—which is characterized by liberation—is appropriate. This too is incorrect.

Since the state of being the substratum of liberation exists only in that which is qualified by liberation, it has been stated that because [liberation] appears in its form as pure consciousness through the sentence of dispute (*vipratipatti-vākya*), it is only that which is so qualified which appears; therefore, a dispute regarding that [pure consciousness] is impossible. Furthermore, if you assert that liberation resides in pure consciousness because you accept that the attributes of the qualified reside in the pure, then difference (*bheda*) also certainly resides there; how then could there be a disagreement concerning that alternative?

Furthermore, having accepted that there is no difference whatsoever in pure consciousness (*śuddhacit*), if you think that—by establishing mere difference in pure consciousness as the locus for proving difference in that which is characterized by liberation—the purpose of the self (*ātman*) is fulfilled through this counter-argument (*vipratipatti*) regarding the absence of difference in that characterized by liberation; then, by following some property such as "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) or "state of being a transmigrator" (*saṃsāritva*) as the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), it is possible to establish difference in consciousness [even without the specific qualification], and thus your position is vitiated by the very fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

There is an inconsistency in pursuing "being liberated from saṃsāra" as the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) after having refuted that [liberation]. If, however, one follows the view of the *Vivaraṇa*—which holds that just like properties such as purity (*śuddhatva*), the exclusions of the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the unreal (*anṛta*) also reside in pure consciousness (*śuddhaciti*) itself—then there is no contradiction, because difference is admitted in pure consciousness alone. Nor is the purpose of the inference fulfilled by proving that [difference], since the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) has not been avoided. Furthermore, there is no contradiction regarding the two alternatives of difference and its absence with respect to that which is qualified by liberation (*muktatva*).

In my view, since there is no dispute regarding the difference [of the self] as qualified by liberation—which consists in the destruction of the veil (āvaraṇadhvaṃsa) occurring at the final moment or through the final direct realization—it is also not reasonable to maintain a disagreement concerning that which is qualified by the state of being liberated, defined as being characterized by the state following that [realization]. This is because, in my view, that subsequent state itself is unreal (alīka). Furthermore, if liberation were merely consciousness (cit) characterized by the destruction of the veil, then, due to the absence of a substratum for it, it would be unfit to serve as the delimiting condition (pakṣatāvacchedaka) of the subject.

Furthermore, if there is a dispute regarding difference as an unrestricted qualifier based on a locus of liberation established for both parties, then even if difference were to be proven by that very relation, there would be neither an illogicality in the dispute nor the fallacy of proving what is already established; for difference, which is perishing in liberation, does not exist as an unrestricted qualifier in consciousness.

Nor should it be suspected that there is a sublation (*bādha*) or a lack of proof for the example (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*) because the distinctness-qualifier residing in the subject (*pakṣa*) or the example is delimited by properties such as "being released" or "being bound with shackles. This is because you must include in the definition precisely that which is not the determiner (*anirūpaka*) of that specific kind of delimitation (*avacchedakatā*) which functions as time (*kāla*). Even that [position] is incorrect.

Since I have accepted that the qualification of distinctions such as "unreality" (anṛta), which persist for as long as *saṃsāra* lasts, consists precisely in their being temporally unrestricted (*kālānavacchinna*) due to their being temporally pervasive occurrences (*kālikavyāpyavṛtti*), the objections of "inconsistency" (*vipratipatti*) and "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) remain unrefuted. Nor should it be asked how distinctions not connected to the time of liberation can possess temporal pervasiveness; for since time itself is sublated along with the distinctions by the knowledge of Brahman, time simply does not exist at the state of liberation.

Nor should it be argued that there would be no contradiction in not admitting time in the case of liberation; for when there is no disagreement, the objection of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) arises, and since the mere acceptance of an opponent's view—whether examined or unexamined—is the basis [for such objections], any inquiry into its existence or non-existence is now precluded by the lack of occasion. Furthermore, in this alternative, if the general property of consciousness residing in the self, such as "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) or "being in saṃsāra" (*saṃsāritva*), could also serve as the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), then one cannot avoid the previously mentioned fault consisting in the impossibility of abandoning it.

If it is argued that since you have accepted the non-existence of difference (*bhedābhāva*) for the sake of establishing the falsity of difference, it is logical for that [non-existence] to be a position in the debate (*koṭi*), we say no. Because that [non-existence] is currently obscured, it is not an object of cognition for ordinary people that contradicts their acceptance of difference; thus, since it cannot resolve the doubt of a neutral observer, it is unfit to be a position in the dispute. Furthermore, even when proving difference, the very position we intend to establish would be proven, and thus the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) would remain unremoved.

"Therefore, since it is impossible for there to be a misconception regarding a subject that is free from the extreme of being a pure difference, how could there be an absence of *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) at that time by means of proving difference?"—this is the resolution.

To this it is replied: There are certain statements such as "the supreme goal of the liberated," "even though they have resorted to His body, they have attained the Supreme Viṣṇu which is the goal of the liberated," and "having attained My own nature, they are not born even at the time of creation, nor do they suffer at the time of dissolution"; likewise, Vedic passages such as "having approached this Self consisting of bliss" and "He attains the highest equality" are heard, understood as referring to the state of liberation.

Likewise, there are Vedic statements such as, "He who knows the supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman," and "But where everything has become his very Self. Similarly:
"Until liberation, there must indeed be a distinction between the individual soul and the supreme;
but for the liberated one, there is no distinction, due to the absence of any cause for distinction."
When the ignorance that produces the sense of duality has gone to absolute destruction,
who will bring about the unreal distinction between the Self and Brahman?
As long as there is liberation, there may be a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme;
beyond that, however, no distinction exists, due to the absence of any cause for distinction.

These and other scriptural passages from the Smṛti are understood to refer to the state of liberation. In those preceding passages, the distinction between liberated souls among themselves and between them and the Supreme Self is apprehended through the hearing of the plural number, as well as through the similarity [of attributes] and the hearing of the relationship between that which is attained and that which attains. However, in passages such as "But where [he is]... (*yatra tv asya...*), the state of liberation is indicated by the word "where" (*yatra*); the time subsequent to that [liberation] is indicated by the phrases "when he has gone to absolute destruction" (*nāśam ātyantikam gate*) and "after that" (*tataḥ param*).

Thus, by the statements "everything became the Self alone" and "there is no duality," the negation of duality in general is perceived. When there is a state of indecision regarding the relative strength or weakness of these two types of passages—while those among your own followers who follow Bhāskara say, "Since those passages teaching duality lack authority because they intend another meaning, the passages concerning non-duality are the valid authorities," and while the proponents of truth (Tattvavādins) say, "The passages intended to negate duality do not have their own literal meaning as their primary purpose, but rather intend another meaning"—[the following applies].

Among worldly people, including those who are neutral, does the doubt arise—"Is he liberated, or is he not liberated?"—or does it not? One who says "it does not" is a denier of what is established by universal experience; such a person is neither a follower of the Vedas nor a worldly person, and thus should simply be ignored.

In the first case, since that which is qualified by the destruction of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and that which is qualified by the time subsequent to it appear as the subjects (*dharmin*) through the two sentences that negate difference, doubt arises precisely therein; and when there is a desire to know one or the other of those two, there is no room for the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) in the proof of difference regarding that which is qualified by the stated delimitors of the scope of the subject of dispute, such as being liberated or being delimited by the time of liberation.

[Objection: But surely, I do accept a difference [of the self] characterized by the destruction of bondage; however, since the time subsequent to that [destruction] is not accepted, it has already been stated that its being the subject (*pakṣatā*)—as delimited by that [time]—is improper due to its non-establishment. [Reply: This is not so.

For if one accepts a difference in the qualified entity [the self as characterized by the destruction of bondage], then the scriptural statements "He attains similarity" (*sādharmyam āgatā*) and "Supreme equality" (*paramaṃ sāmyam*) would imply that "similarity and supreme equality are indeed non-difference. Likewise, the statement "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman" (*so 'śnute sarvān kāmān saha brahmaṇā vipaścitā*) would mean, "O best of gods, he enjoys all desires sequentially. *Note: The argument here concerns the ontological status of the liberated self. The opponent argues that if liberation involves a temporal sequence (such as the destruction of bondage followed by a state of similarity), then the subject of the inference cannot be established, as the post-liberation state is not admitted. The proponent counters that if one accepts a difference in the qualified self, then scriptural passages describing "similarity" or "equality" must be interpreted as signifying non-difference, which contradicts the opponent's own position.*
Having realized the nature of Brahman, he is undoubtedly liberated while living.

Having cited such passages from the *Skanda Purāṇa*, an interpretation that takes them to mean the experience of all enjoyments through the very nature of Brahman would render the explanation of the word "upetya" in the passage "having approached the Self consisting of bliss" as meaning "not transgressing" (an-atikrama) entirely redundant. Nor can it be argued that even if other forms of difference are admitted, since the difference from Brahman is not admitted, it is appropriate to interpret those passages understood to have that [non-difference] as their purport.

For when ignorance itself is absolutely destroyed, it is impossible for any other form of difference to persist—just as the difference from Brahman cannot persist—and furthermore, it is impossible for that which is qualified by another difference to attain identity with Brahman. Moreover, the intended meaning of "identity of essential nature" is not applicable specifically to liberation, since it is already undifferentiated even during the state of transmigratory existence.

Furthermore, what is gained for you by the statement that establishes a difference between Brahman? If you say it is the authority of such statements as "He becomes Brahman itself," then how can you accept another kind of difference that contradicts the authority of statements such as "But for the liberated one, there is no difference"? Nor can it be argued that the purport of those statements lies in the negation of difference, or in pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), or in some other restrictive rule such as "having the same object" and so forth; for you cannot accept [that difference] on the grounds that it does not contradict the meaning that constitutes the actual purport of the texts.

In that case, since the same interpretation applies to statements such as "he becomes Brahman itself," why have you proposed an alternative explanation for the aforementioned scriptural passages? Therefore, your view remains exactly as it was heard: that there is no difference [between the soul and Brahman] once the state of liberation is attained.

Just as it is accepted that sentences such as "not here, not there" (neha nānā) have the pure consciousness (cinmātra) as their ultimate purport by means of establishing the general absence of duality, and that sentences such as "that thou art" (tattvamasi) have the pure consciousness as their ultimate purport by means of conveying non-difference through secondary signification (lakṣaṇā)—and that the knowledge of consciousness mediated by those [sentences] is opposed to the cognition of duality—for that purpose, the purport of those sentences resides even in the mediated knowledge; they possess a conventional validity (vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya) constituted by that object, in order to establish the purport of those sentences toward such intermediate knowledge.

This is because of your own statement: "The operation of fallacious inferences and non-difference inferences [is directed] against one who disputes the meaning of such scriptural passages as 'There is no diversity here,' and thus he states another probandum. Similarly, you must accept that sentences negating the difference between liberated souls (mukta) either have as their purport the negation of difference in that which is qualified by liberation, or they have as their purport the rule that ultimately negates everything.

In order to maintain empirical validity (*vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya*) regarding the meaning that constitutes the intermediate intention (*avāntaratātparya*), one must accept that the absence of difference (*bhedābhāva*) qualified by liberation exists; furthermore, all time—whether it be the state of liberation described in the passage "But when for him," or the time subsequent to that described in the passage "Thereafter," which is not delimited by any general difference and is delimited by the cessation of ignorance—must be accepted as being projected by the ignorance of bound persons during the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāradaśā*).
This has been stated in the *Advaitacandrikā* in the determination of the reason for insentience (*jaḍatva*): "Because the time of liberation, which is projected by bound persons, is admitted."

And thus, just as the respective proofs for our two positions are established regarding the world—which you yourself accept as being indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*)—by means of a dispute (*vipratipatti*) concerning the alternatives of falsity (*mithyātva*) and reality (*satyatva*), which constitute the scope of the secondary purport (*avāntara-tātparya*) of the scripture; so too, according to your own view, the dispute concerning the alternatives of difference and non-difference is indeed appropriate, because [the world] is established by the aforementioned reasoning as being characterized by the destruction of its concealment (*āvaraṇa-dhvaṃsa*), delimited by that specific time, and delimited by the time subsequent thereto.

However, the qualified entity that is the subject of our disagreement is either indeterminable for you or real for me, Bhāskara; in that case, our desired conclusion is established merely by proving the difference [between them].

Since the scriptural passages that negate difference are—according to my view—subject to the same status as the scriptural passages on falsity (in that they must be interpreted as having a different meaning due to their contradiction with other scriptural texts supported by reasoning), the mediating cognition is not established; and since even your intended refined meaning is thus unestablished, your defeat has indeed occurred. Therefore, difference is accepted in consciousness. What is the use of your prattle, "I accept difference in something qualified"?

Alternatively, let your acceptance of the matter be as it may; nevertheless, since a doubt has arisen due to the aforementioned conflict among the scriptures, and since there is a risk that one might follow merely the shadow of your own opinion and thus fail to negate the category of difference—therefore, when such a doubt has been reached, this formal application of logic (*nyāyaprayoga*) has been made in general terms. This logic is composed of words that provide the counter-correlates (*pratiyogi*) for the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) found in those scriptural statements, and it functions by means of dismantling the sentence-meanings favored by the opponent in order to bring about the ascertainment of reality (*tattvanirṇaya*) for the disciples through the negation of difference.

And thus, when there is a disagreement based on following the scriptures exactly as they were heard, the logical statement is that "the one under dispute is different," which conforms strictly to what was heard in the scriptures. However, if one were to respect the refined meaning intended by you [the opponent] regarding the scriptures, then that meaning—provided it takes the form of the aforementioned restriction—would merely be a restatement of a worldly fact, even though such a restriction is established through common worldly practice; for it is possible for it to be a restatement of a worldly matter, just like those scriptures that teach the causal relationship between the direct realization of the Self and the cessation of ignorance.

Since activity is possible only for the sake of realizing that [truth] while it is yet unestablished, let the purport of the root statement be this: regarding the doubt—whether or not the moment constituting the locus of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) is preceded by a time that is the locus of a visible object (dṛśya) caused by ignorance (ajñāna) which is co-located with and has the same object as the knowledge of reality residing in itself—the proof of its non-existence is the inference based on the root statement. In either case, there is no room for the charge of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) against you.

Nor can it be argued that the non-existence of ignorance is unestablished because positive ignorance is unestablished in your own system; for since you have designated *prakṛti* itself as ignorance, its non-existence is not unestablished. Even so, it must be admitted that the existence of ignorance remains unestablished, because you do not accept that it has itself as its object.

Against the Naiyāyikas and others, at the time of the presentation of conflicting views (*vipratipatti*), in order to avoid the objection that the alternative intended as "being of the nature of absence" (*abhāvarūpatva*) is unestablished due to the non-apprehension of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*), and in order to avoid the objection of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) against me, one must accept the following: the rule that true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) necessarily lacks the state of being preceded by a time that is the locus of that which is visible (*dṛśya*) and is produced by that [knowledge] which is directly opposed to it. Here, "opposition" (*virodhitva*) means being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of the destruction produced by itself.

And this can be somehow resolved by the following line of reasoning: it is well-known in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) that it is destroyed by its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), according to the view that holds such destruction; thus, the establishment of my position within the category of positive entities (*bhāvakoṭi*) is easily achieved.

Alternatively, having introduced difference (*bheda*) as delimited by the nature of self-realization (*ātmasākṣātkāratva*), or as difference-in-general (*bhedatva*), or as being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*), there arises a dispute (*vipratipatti*) whose one alternative consists in its occurrence prior to the time of that substratum, and whose other alternative consists in its non-existence in a state of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*). Among these, the positive alternative belongs to the proponents of ultimate reality (*tatvavādinaḥ*), while the negative alternative belongs to the proponents of Māyā (*māyāvādinaḥ*), because the establishment of their intended object follows merely from the establishment of that [difference] in some instance of realization.

The purport of the probans-statement (*hetuvākya*) is that the cause of either bondage or its destruction is the state of existing at a time that is the locus of the destruction of bondage—which is of the nature of suffering—either through the relation of existing at a time that is the locus of its own destruction, or through the relation of existing at a time that is the locus of itself.

Since true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) consists in the eradication of all that is visible (*dṛśya*), with respect to the final direct intuition (*caramasākṣātkāra*) taken as the moment of true knowledge, or elsewhere with respect to the destruction of another instance of suffering, the probans remains uncontradicted (*anapavāda*) by virtue of being delimited by the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

Furthermore, if it is maintained that the final cognition of reality (*tattvajñāna*) consists in the destruction of all visible objects other than itself, and if—on the view that the second moment of that [cognition], or the self delimited by it, constitutes the destruction of that cognition of reality—it is thereby accepted that the cognition of reality persists for two moments; then, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) with respect to the probandum defined by the inclusion of difference by way of "being visible" (*dṛśyatva*), one must take as the locus the very same [second moment] of the cognition of reality.

The probandum (*sādhya*) is either "the state of being perceivable" (*dṛśyatva*) related by the relation of "having a common locus in a moment that is the substratum of a true cognition occurring prior to the time whose substratum is itself," or "the state of existing in a moment prior to a moment that is the substratum of the perceivable."

Furthermore, if even when the probandum is established by way of a specific delimitant (*avacchedaka-avacchedena*), there is indeed the fault of partial *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established), then otherwise—according to the literal method—it would be possible to avoid *siddhasādhana* by taking "being released from shackles" and so forth as the probandum, since it is not established with respect to the delimitant of "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) or the delimitant of "liberation" (*muktatva*). In that case, pursuing the status of being the subject (*pakṣatā*) up to "one liberated from saṃsāra" would be useless. Thus, even in the refined formulation, it is more appropriate to follow that very [literal] opinion.

And thus, since the direct realization of the self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*) is established as being precisely that [ultimate] reality, if one were to say that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking as the subject the present perception of the self included within the category of the "thesis" (*pakṣa*), then—either by defining it as a realization not co-temporal with the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of suffering co-located with itself, or by defining it as a realization possessing the difference from whatever is co-temporal with the prior absence of the transformation of the mind (*manas*) which serves as its own material cause—the final realization alone constitutes the subject; therefore, there is no room for the fallacy of proving what is already established or other such defects.

In this context, whether in the previous formulation (*pūrvakalpa*) or the present one, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by means of the doctrine of the plurality of souls (*bahujīvavāda*), the qualification of "subsisting in the same locus as itself" (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*) must be refined by being applied either to the cognition or to the difference (*bheda*). And "subsisting in the same locus as itself" means residing in the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) of that [cognition]. Therefore, even though in the final system (*siddhānta*) differences residing in the Self (*ātman*) do not reside in the mental modification (*vṛtti*) which is the substratum of the direct perception, there is no defect. By this, it is also refuted that [the opponent's objection]—namely, that if the subject (*pakṣa*) is defined as the direct perception of the Self having an unconditioned objective reference residing in the Self (*anavacchinnātmaniṣṭhaviṣayatāka*), then the subject is unestablished (*pakṣāsiddhi*) because the proponent of reality (*tatvavādin*) does not admit such a cognition.

The objection that "if the subject (*pakṣa*) is defined as the knowledge that is the intended object of such scriptural passages as 'merely by seeing Him, one is liberated,' then—even according to the Tattvavādin school—liberation is delayed due to the delay in the grace of the Lord even after the attainment of immediate (*aparokṣa*) knowledge; thus, while the stated probandum exists in such knowledge during the period of *saṃsāra*, time and difference are not established at the moment of liberation, and consequently, the author's own position fails"—is refuted. This is because only those [knowledges] occurring in the moment immediately preceding liberation constitute the subject. Furthermore, to exclude the innate self-knowledge (*svarūpa-jñāna*) existing during the period of *saṃsāra*, the qualification of being merely "produced" (*janyatva*) should be adopted.

Furthermore, if you do not accept that the aforementioned scriptural passages and their supporting arguments are intended to establish the stated restriction, then whatever meaning and purpose you consider them to have, our own reasoning is also accepted as establishing a meaning contrary to that and serving a purpose contrary to it; thus, there is no room whatsoever for fallacies such as *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established). This is the general direction [of the argument].

However, some say: "If, out of sheer audacity, you claim that there is a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) merely by your own admission, then you should be satisfied with the fact that even that [admission] is false according to your own view, and thus its absence exists. Nor should it be argued that the absence of *siddhasādhana* must be one that is non-co-locus with its counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*), for even that is present as something superimposed upon the dull-witted. Nor should it be argued that what is required there is a conventional reality (*vyāvahārikatva*) or a state of being other than the illusory (*prātibhāsika*), for even that is present as imagined by the dull-witted."

In reality, however, according to the opponent's own view, it is only after the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of the silver in the mother-of-pearl and similar cases has been established that the inference—"the subject of dispute is false"—proceeds. The fact that this inference is stated in the text before that [establishment of indeterminability], rather than at the outset, is for the purpose of demonstrating the logical consistency of this inference by dispelling the misconception that it is inconsistent.

In the same way, following the refutation of the inferential means (*anumāna*) regarding the category of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) and the indeterminability of the world, this [present] discussion proceeds by way of a disagreement concerning the mere difference between the liberated soul and [the Supreme Self], according to the method already stated. Hereafter, for the sake of instructing the disciples, this treatise is undertaken to somehow establish the consistency of this [discussion] with the aforementioned inference, thereby removing any suspicion of inconsistency.

Furthermore, even the opponent will state in the conclusion of his own work regarding the establishment of the "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*): "Thus, when the indefinable is established, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*). Therefore, according to the view of the proponent of the indefinable, there is no room for the charge of *siddhasādhana* by taking difference within pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as the subject. Consequently, one should not suspect that the aforementioned inconsistency remains—on the grounds that even when taking the Self alone as the subject, the opponent would be unable to raise the objection of *siddhasādhana* based on conventional difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*).

Even if that were the case, since there is a dispute regarding the difference in the liberated state, the proof of difference with respect to the self alone would constitute the fault of "stating what is not desired" (*anākāṅkṣitābhidhāna*), which is a form of irrelevance (*asaṅgati*). Furthermore, we consider it correct to regard "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhanatā*) as a fault from that very perspective within our own system (*siddhānta*).

However, some say: "For the Advaitins, difference (bheda) is intended as the probandum (sādhya) by means of the relation of qualified-qualification (viśeṣaṇatā), characterized by being delimited by a moment that is the locus of the prior absence of its own locus-time, and which terminates in the Self as delimited by the final moment (caramakṣaṇa)—that is, the moment delimited by the locus of bondage when it has reached the state of perishing. Since the aforementioned inference does not reach its conclusion without both time and difference in liberation, there is the establishment of both time and difference."

That is questionable. For there is no evidence that the very final moment favored by the Advaitin is indeed his own intended final moment; if, for the Advaitin, the present moment itself is apprehended as being the final one, then even if the probandum (sādhya) is established in that [present] moment delimited by that [finality] through the aforementioned relation, difference would remain unestablished in liberation according to his own view. Nor is this a welcome conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it has been stated that this discussion takes the form of a formal debate (*vāda*); and since the nature of a formal debate cannot be established in the absence of a determination of truth, a welcome conclusion is inappropriate.
Otherwise, it would result in the discussion being a mere destructive argument (*vitaṇḍā*).

Furthermore, even for the Advaitin, since they accept the aforementioned probandum (sādhya) as imagined by a bound person within the aforementioned subject (pakṣa), the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) remains unavoidable. If one follows the aforementioned subject precisely according to its literal meaning, there is a contradiction with the *Ṭīkā*, which states, "one who is liberated from saṃsāra is intended [as the subject]," and it is evident that the very reason of liberation (*muktatva*), which was explicitly stated in the root text, would have to be abandoned exactly as it stands in its literal sense. Therefore, the charge of *siddhasādhana* must be avoided by placing a burden upon the term "disputed" (*vimata*) according to the method we have described. What is the use of adhering to a probandum constructed with a relation not accepted in our own system? Enough!

However, some maintain that liberation in the form of the destruction of the bondage consisting of ignorance itself serves as the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) by way of a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Just as when something functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)—that is, as the delimiting factor of the intended object (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*)—the co-temporality of the delimiting factor and the predicate (*vidheya*) appears [in cognition], so too it is accepted that in cases where something is a delimiting factor by way of being a secondary indicator, the posteriority of the delimiting factor relative to the intended object appears in the predicate.

Nor should it be argued that the manifestation of simultaneity is unauthenticated simply because a difference between the cases of the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) and the characterized (*upalakṣita*) can be established merely by the non-manifestation of simultaneity. For the logic is the same: if a difference between the two cases can be established merely by the non-manifestation of posteriority in the case of the characterized, then there is no evidence for the manifestation of simultaneity in the case where [the qualifier] manifests as a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*). Nor should it be argued that the relation of the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) manifests in that latter case.

This is because there is no evidence for a relationship of delimitum and delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) other than that of being simultaneous. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that the cognition produced by the current sentence "The red pot stands" would be invalid—on the grounds that in the case of a thing characterized (*upalakṣita*), the delimiting property of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) is understood as subsequent [to the characterization], and thus there is an intention to convey the cognition of a pot characterized by redness with the desire to express its future state of being red; for such an outcome is actually desired. And it has been stated by your own [teachers]:
"The cessation of delusion is the Self, characterized by the nature of knowledge."

Thus, in the course of explaining the *Vārttika*, [the author] takes the case of future knowledge (*bhāvi-jñāna*) as an example to preclude the conventional usage of the cessation of ignorance (*ajñāna-nivṛtti*) for the self at the present time, stating: "In its own prior time, there is no such thing as being a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇatva*) for itself; for one does not employ the term 'cook' (*pācaka*) with the intention that it be a qualifier during the time prior to the act of cooking.

If even such a usage were considered authoritative, then one must admit either that only the non-appearance of simultaneity and posteriority is what is manifested therein, or else that the state of being a qualifier—consisting in existing at the time of its own prior absence—is what is manifested.

The specific determinants (*niyāmaka-viśeṣa*), however, are as follows: in the case of verbal cognition, they consist in the apprehension of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) in various ways; elsewhere, they consist in the consideration of the absence of sublation (*bādhādy-abhāva-parāmarśa*), sensory contact (*indriya-sannikarṣa*), and so forth. As has been stated, in an inference that apprehends a difference with respect to what is characterized by the aforementioned delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), the state of occurring after liberation (*mukty-uttarakālikatva*) appears in the difference. Therefore, there is no room for the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). Nor should it be asked why, in that case, the state of occurring prior [to liberation] does not appear.

They say: "Just as the apprehension of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs only after the apprehension of the sublation of the primary meaning, by the force of experience, so too in all cases, the status of being a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇatva*) consisting of posteriority appears only after the determination of the sublation of the status of being a qualifier consisting of priority. And in the present case, because there is no such sublation, priority does not appear; rather, only posteriority appears."

As for the argument that "because it is the very nature of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend ultimate existence, ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) appears in [the cognition of] difference; therefore, the inference does not suffer from the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*)"; this, however, must be considered, because it would entail the consequence that there is no reason to abandon the subject (*pakṣa*) as delimited by selfhood (*ātmatva*) and so forth.

Nor is the restriction stated by you—beginning with "nor of the knowledge of reality"—tenable. For instance, is this restriction intended in a form common to the knowledge of liberation and so forth, or is it based on the aforementioned scriptures and restricted solely to the knowledge of the reality of the Self? It cannot be the first; for if you say that "the nature of the knowledge of reality" means "validity" (*pramātva*), then that very term must be defined.

If it is argued that [validity] consists in the cognition’s having as its object that which possesses the property [in question], then even cognitions such as "this is silver" would have to be considered valid, because they too have as their objects things possessing silver and so forth through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). Consequently, since the pervader—the absence of ignorance whose object is identical to itself—is unestablished there due to the presence of the pervaded [validity], there is a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Furthermore, this definition fails to include the knowledge of the Self (*ātman*) which is devoid of any qualifying attributes (*niṣprakāraka*). Nor can validity consist in having an uncontradicted object as its domain; for having an object that is uncontradicted for some time is common even to the cognition of "silver in a shell" (*śuktirūpya*).

In no way does the property of having as its object a content that is non-sublated exist even in the cognition of mother-of-pearl [as silver]. Nor should it be argued that "the state of apprehending an object that is not sublated at the time of practical transaction" (vyavahārakālābādhyārthāvagāhitva) amounts to "not being sublated by anything other than the knowledge of Brahman," because even though the Self—which is entirely non-sublatable—possesses this quality of not being sublated during the time of practical transaction, the definition would fail to include the cognition of that Self;

for there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the error regarding the identity of the body and the self, since that entity, which is the object of an error whose sublation has not yet occurred prior to the direct realization of Brahman, would also [falsely] possess that same status.

Nor is it the case that "being the object of a different [type of] gross ignorance" (tūlājñāna) constitutes that [definition]. If "gross ignorance-ness" (tūlājñānatva) were defined as "being sublated by something other than the knowledge of Brahman," then there would be a logical fallacy (vyabhicāra), because even those ignorances that produce the aforementioned delusions regarding objects would likewise be so sublated; consequently, the delusions apprehending those objects produced by such ignorances would also result in being considered valid cognitions (pramā), which would entail the undesirable consequence that such [delusions] could remove ignorance. If it is argued that "gross ignorance-ness" is a genus (jāti) subordinate to the genus "ignorance-ness" (avidyātva), we reply that this is untenable, because there is no evidence for the very existence of the genus "ignorance-ness," and thus, a fortiori, there is no evidence for a genus subordinate to it.

Even if one accepts a distinct species (*vaijātya*) residing in the ignorance of the cotton-wool (*tūla-ajñāna*), there would still be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a valid sublation (*bādhapramā*) that arises on the first day following the error "this is silver," where subsequently, on the second day, the error "this is silver" occurs again. This is because, in accordance with the error arising on the second day, another instance of ignorance must necessarily be admitted there; and since that [new ignorance] has the same object as itself and is co-located with it, it would possess the same objective content and locus as the original.

Likewise, there is a deviation [from the proposed rule] even at the time when the ignorance that produces a dream-illusion on the second day—possessing an object identical to its own and residing in the same substratum—is still present, following the awakening from a previous dream-illusion; for there is no difference in the objects of the ignorances producing the dream-illusions of the preceding and succeeding days, as there is a lack of evidence [for such a difference] and because [such a distinction] is difficult to establish. Furthermore, there is a deviation from the stated rule regarding pearls and other items given in a dream, which are sometimes perceived even after waking up.

Nor can it be said that these [dream-cognitions] are not caused by ignorance (*ajñāna*), but rather are caused specifically by *mūlājñāna* (radical ignorance). For there is no evidence that those cognitions which arise independently of external causal conditions are caused by *mūlājñāna*.

Furthermore, if ignorance has the same object as knowledge—that is, if its object is the object of knowledge—then what is that knowledge? Is it the mental modification (*vṛtti*), or is it the consciousness reflected therein (*tatpratibimbitacaitanya*)? It cannot be the first. On this view, is the objectivity (*viṣayatā*) called "form" (*ākāra*) secondary (*gauṇī*), or is it primary (*mukhyā*) in the form of identity (*tādātmya*)? It cannot be the first.

The first [alternative] is untenable because the secondary objectivity (*gauṇaviṣayatā*) termed "aspect" (*ākāra*), which belongs to the direct perception having "shell-ness" (*śuktitva*) as its qualifier, exists only in the shell (*śakti*) and so forth; whereas the objectivity termed "aspect" belonging to ignorance (*ajñāna*) whose object is consciousness delimited by that [shell] does not exist there. Consequently, it is impossible for the two to have the same object. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because since the identity (*tādātmya*) with the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is not admitted in the case of consciousness delimited by the shell, that same defect remains as before. Nor is it of the nature of consciousness reflected in the mental modification (*vṛtti*).

This is because, since the objective state (*viṣayatā*) whose nature is identity with that [object] does not exist within consciousness (*cit*), it is impossible for ignorance regarding consciousness to have that same object. Now, "having the same object" means: being an objective state determined by a delimitation (*avacchedakatā*) which is qualified by its own mode (*prakāratā*). And the qualification of the delimitation by the mode occurs through two relations: co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and homogeneity (*sajātīyatva*). Homogeneity, in turn, is by way of either being delimited or non-delimited by something residing in itself.

If it is argued that there is identity of object between the ignorance whose object is consciousness limited by "shell-ness" (śuktitva) as qualified by it, and the cognition of the shell—because the "shell-ness-ness" (śuktitvatva) residing in the mode of the cognition of shell-ness exists within the delimitation of the objectivity residing in shell-ness (which is itself delimited by the objectivity of the ignorance residing in the consciousness of the shell)—by means of both relations [of inherence and being delimited by], then [we reply]: since the cognition of Brahman is devoid of modes (niṣprakāraka), and because the relation of the root-ignorance residing in consciousness is non-delimited (anavacchinna).

In that case, there is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the non-establishment of the pervader (*vyāpaka*). If "having a mode" (*saprakāratva*) is included in the definition of the pervaded (*vyāpya*), then the knowledge of Brahman and the cognitions produced by sentences such as "This is that Devadatta" would not be included. Furthermore, since the cognition "The mountain is luminous" would have the same object as the ignorance whose object is consciousness delimited by the qualified object—the mountain possessing fire as qualified by the property of firehood—there would follow the undesirable consequence of a relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*nivartya-nivartaka-bhāva*).

Furthermore, there is the impossibility of co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the ignorance that prevents manifestation—which resides in consciousness delimited by the object—and the knowledge residing in the knower. If you argue for co-location by asserting that the mental modification (vṛtti) of the internal organ, having gone out through the eyes and other senses, resides in the consciousness delimited by the object, then the specification [of the ignorance as residing in the same locus] would be non-excluding, because it would result in the co-location of Caitra’s ignorance with Maitra’s knowledge.

If one accepts that ignorance is defined by Caitra and others, and instead of co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya) introduces "being defined by its own substratum" (svāśrayanirūpitatva), then since the ignorance residing in the knower is established through co-location alone, there is no proof for its being defined by the knower (pramātṛnirūpitatva); consequently, its cessation cannot be established. Even if another restrictive rule were accepted in that case, the aforementioned defect remains unavoidable in instances where a single person possesses multiple ignorances that produce many cognitions of the same kind.

By this, the following view is also refuted: "The objectivity termed 'aspect' (ākāra) is one and the same for both knowledge and ignorance; this is admitted even in the case of insentient objects. Thus, having the same object consists simply in being the determiner of an objectivity that is itself determined by [the cognition]. This is because the aforementioned counter-example remains unavoidable.

As for the argument that "since it is accepted that each respective cognition is the destroyer of its corresponding ignorance, and since it is admitted that true cognitions (*tattvajñāna*) have the property of being removed by themselves when this is attributed to ignorance, there is no deviation from the previously stated rule anywhere," that is incorrect. For it would result in the redundancy of the conditions of "co-occurrence in the same locus" (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*) and "having the same object" (*svasamānaviṣayakatva*). Furthermore, what kind of "being caused by ignorance" (*ajñānaprayuktatva*) is included in the rule regarding visible objects?

[The definition of superimposition] must be either (1) having that as its material cause (*upādāna*), or (2) being directly produced by it, or (3) being produced [by it] in a manner common to both direct and indirect production, or (4) consisting of a specific relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*). It cannot be the first, because by the force of the aforementioned rule, it would follow that beginningless objects of perception—such as time, the ignorance consisting of the form of time, the relation between consciousness and ignorance, and the distinction between the individual self (*jīva*) and Brahman—would not exist even in liberation; yet this is not established. For this very reason, it cannot be the second.

Furthermore, because it is accepted that after the direct realization of the Self (*ātma-aparokṣa*), there remain objects whose material cause is subliminal impression (*saṃskāra*) due to the dissolution of only those objects rooted in ignorance (*āvidyaka*), one cannot establish the total abolition of all visible phenomena (*dṛśya-sāmānya-uccheda*) in liberation even by taking those [impression-based objects] into account; thus, the futility of accepting the stated rule in both positions is unavoidable. Moreover, in the second position—where the view is held that a known inferential mark (*liṅga*) is the cause of inference—there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since an inference in Maitra based on the mark of Caitra’s ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl would still exist even after Caitra’s direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of that mother-of-pearl. Nor is the third position tenable.

Because the previously mentioned defects have not been avoided; and because there is a deviation [in the definition], since fear and the like arising from the error of a snake—which are produced by the non-cognition of the rope through a causal chain—persist even after the direct perception of the rope. Nor is it the fourth [alternative]; for even if one somehow accepts that beginningless objects of perception possess "being caused" (prayuktatva) in the form of a relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*), which is common to all beginningless things despite their lacking production either directly or indirectly, the deviation pointed out in the third position remains unavoidable.

Furthermore, even in the case of fear and the like, there is no loss of their being produced by a relationship consisting in their essential nature, as evidenced by the cognition: "All this undesirable [state] of mine arose from the non-cognition of the rope. Moreover, since there would be no proof for the fact that things whose material cause (*upādāna*) is the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance are themselves produced by ignorance, it would follow that the destruction of those [impressions] could not be established.

As for the claim that "beginningless objects of perception are caused by ignorance (*avidyā*) and are counter-correlates of destruction dependent upon the destruction of ignorance; since this does not apply to the aforementioned fear and so forth, there is no deviation [in the rule]," that is trivial. Since the doctrine of Pure Non-duality (*śuddhādvaita*) is what is being accepted here, if one admits the destruction of beginningless objects of perception through the destruction of ignorance, then by admitting the destruction of destruction itself, non-duality is lost. Even if one imagines the Self to have that nature (of being destructible), the same fault remains if the imagined destruction within it is not itself annihilated.

If one postulates another destruction for destruction itself, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā) resulting from the postulation of an unauthentic series of destructions.
