Having himself stated that "the acceptance of the view that knowledge of reality delimited by the first moment is the destruction of ignorance, while that same [knowledge] delimited by the second moment is produced as the cessation of the flowing manifest world—whether beginningless or beginningless—is to be rejected because it leads to the consequence that knowledge of reality does not destroy ignorance," he has respected the intent of the Śrutis and other authorities regarding the aforementioned rule.

In that regard, since the very process of [the view] that the destruction of all beginningless objects of perception is caused by the destruction of ignorance has been abandoned, it is impossible to include within the body of such a restrictive rule (niyama) the notion of "being necessitated," which consists in being the counter-positive of a destruction necessitated by the destruction of ignorance. Therefore, it is not tenable that the restrictive rule applies here according to the first method. Nor is the second alternative previously considered—namely, that the rule applies only in the case of the direct realization of the Self on the strength of scripture and other authorities—correct; for even here, under the position that accepts the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance, the fault of the rule's redundancy is unavoidable.

Moreover, this rule must be stated only under the view that there is a plurality of individual souls (jīva) corresponding to the plurality of individual ignorances (avidyā). For, under the view that there is only one ignorance and one soul, the position is already consistent by merely accepting that the moment of self-realization lacks a preceding moment; thus, the rule would be subject to deviation, and the qualifying conditions such as "co-inherent in the same locus" (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*) and so forth, which are intended to prevent such deviation, would be redundant.

And thus, in the view that there are multiple cognitions (*nānājñāna*), even though it is established that Śuka—by virtue of his direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*)—no longer has any connection with the entire world imagined through his own ignorance (*svājñāna*), since he is one among many individual souls (*jīva*) who serve as the material cause of the world; nevertheless, how can liberation be established for him according to the stated rule? For in the alternative view that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is created by the *māyā* of the Lord (*īśvara*), the connections with time and so forth, as well as the connections with the body and so forth, imagined by Maitra and others, do not cease to exist for him, as they are also created by that [Lord]. One’s own ignorance alone brings about some kind of connection for oneself.

If it is argued that liberation is possible because, upon the removal of those [limitations], there is an absence of any relation to anything else, then how can you find occasion to raise the objection of *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) by asserting a distinction in the liberated state?

Furthermore, whether one adopts the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*) or multiple souls (*bahujīvavāda*), and whether the views are common to the world or otherwise, in all these positions, the realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*) must either (1) lack the state of being preceded by a moment that is the locus of the visible (*dṛśya*), or (2) lack the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of a destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) residing in a moment that is the locus of the visible, or (3) not be the locus of a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a moment that is the locus of the visible. In the first case, it results in the final moment being eternal. In the second case as well, it results in the non-arising of any subsequent moment.

Nor should it be argued that if that [liberation] were eternal, its momentariness would be untenable; for even according to you, since you do not admit the destruction of the final moment at a subsequent time, that same defect remains equally applicable to your position as well. Furthermore, if it were possible for the objects of perception to exist after the knowledge of reality—existing like Brahman itself, unconnected with time—then in either case, the total eradication of all perceived phenomena in liberation would remain unestablished. This has been explained in detail elsewhere. Therefore, under the stated rule, if one does not accept time in liberation, the attempt to avoid contradiction is entirely inconsistent.

Furthermore, as for what has been prattled by another: "In proving a difference delimited by the time of liberation, there is the unestablished nature of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) according to the stated method. Proving an ultimate difference is likewise untenable for this very reason. In proving a difference that is not sublated by its own cognition, if the subject (*pakṣa*) is stated by the word 'self' (*sva*), there is the unestablished nature of the probandum; for a difference that is not sublated by the cognition of the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) which constitutes the subject is unestablished."

"In the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), since a conventional difference—which is not sublated by the knowledge of one liberated from the fetters that serve as the example—is admitted in the case of the liberated soul, this is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). As for the argument that 'in Maṇḍana’s view, because the destruction of the final object of perception can occur at the time of liberation, there is no *siddhasādhana* when proving difference in that which is delimited by [the state of] being the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*)', that is not correct; for in his view, since the exclusion of the unreal (*anṛta*) and so forth also exists at the time of liberation, the *siddhasādhana* is unavoidable. This [criticism] is simply unworthy of belief, as it consists of an objection against what was never stated.

Nor is it reasonable to raise an objection on the grounds that these alternative positions are merely conceivable; for if one accepts the stated probandum (*sādhya*), then even if "that which is delimited by selfhood" (*ātmatvāvacchinna*) were taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), there would be no possibility of the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*). Consequently, the rejection of that position would be rendered baseless. Furthermore, from the commentary (*ṭīkā*) passage—"because difference is not qualified by being either ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) or non-conditional (*anaupādhika*)"—which is intended as an illustration of other cases, we understand that the author of the text does not favor the aforementioned alternatives.

Furthermore, regarding the position that "difference uncontradicted by one's own cognition" (*svajñānābādhyabheda*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), the objection raised concerning the ambiguity of the meaning of the word *sva* (self/own) is entirely untenable. To explain: your intention is that such an application of the formal argument (*nyāyaprayoga*) is inconsistent because the probandum cannot be presented in a uniform form; consequently, since there is no comprehension of the probandum in either the subject (*pakṣa*) or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the inference of a neutral observer—mediated by the process of "ascertainment" (*parāmarśa*)—cannot be established. Alternatively, [your objection may be] that while such an application of the argument might work in other cases, it is inconsistent in the present instance.

Not the first [alternative], because it would result in the statement defining your own rule—"of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) which has the same locus," etc.—having the capacity to present only a single instance; consequently, since it would lack the capacity to convey a pervasion (vyāpti) that is common to all cases in every situation, it would result in the fallacy of being incoherent.

Furthermore, since you yourself have refined the reason "being visible" (*dṛśyatva*) by stating "because it possesses visibility that is not sublated by its own cognition," and because in that case too only a single individual (*ekavyakti*) is presented by the word "self" (*sva*), that [refined reason] would also be untenable due to the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*), as it exists only in that one individual. Moreover, logical formulations such as "other than its own prior absence" (*svaprāgabhāvātiriktetyādi*) and conventional usages such as "having an existence not inferior to its own" (*svānyūnasattāketyādi*) are frequently encountered in your own works. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for there is no seed (justification) for such a distinction in the very context under discussion.

Now, if you argue that the mental cognition of the probandum, the reason, and so forth—delimited by the form [of the universal] present therein—arises for the neutral observer after the verbal cognition dependent upon the *nyāya* statement; and that one also understands the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the *nyāya* statement to lie precisely there; and that consequently, through the mediation of the intermediate reflection (*parāmarśa*), the accomplishment of the neutral observer’s inference occurs—then we agree with both of us that, from that statement, all things such as the neutral observer’s inference and the elimination of his doubt are accomplished through the mediation of the neutral observer’s reflection.

As for the manner of establishing that [universal], you have explained it through the manifestation of an underlying property (*anugatadharma*), according to the method stated by you who maintain that linguistic usage cannot be sustained without such a property. However, I, who maintain that everything can be sustained even without an underlying property, explain it in a different way.

For instance, just as when the property of "fire-ness" (vahnitva) is pervasive, the accomplishment of a qualified inferential consideration (viśiṣṭaparāmarśa) occurs—via the cognition of all fires following the cognition of a single fire by way of the property of fire-ness, and via the cognition of pervasion residing in all smoke following that—so too, even in the absence of such pervasiveness, the accomplishment of the qualified inferential consideration is shown in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) to occur through the sense organ aided by the cognition of a distinctive similarity manifested by that property, via the cognition of all fires and so forth.

Just as the universal "fire-ness" (vahnitva), which is the ground for the application of the term "fire," and the universal "substance-ness" (dravyatva), which is the ground for the application of the term "substance," both reside in a single individual, yet they remain mutually unmixed despite the non-difference of their substratum—so it is in all cases for those who maintain the theory of difference-and-non-difference regarding universals and so forth; for us, however, this is another matter, as [the relation] is sometimes by way of difference and sometimes by way of a particularity (viśeṣa).

And thus, since the properties that serve as the grounds for the application of their respective terms among entities are distinct, there is no inconsistency in the accomplishment of the qualified reflective cognition (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*) and so forth, through the apprehension of the pervasions—defined by all the probanda—within the reasons under consideration, by means of the similarity manifested by those [pervasions].

However, by the theory that there is no apprehension of a recurring property (*anugata-dharma*), it is impossible for either the proponent who employs the syllogism containing the word "self" (*sva-śabda*) or the listener to specify [the object] after analysis; thus, one must postulate a relation in some composite entity consisting of various word-meanings that lacks any basis in authority (*aprāmāṇika*). To then postulate that the delimitors of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) and so forth contained therein become objects of the listener's mental cognition, and to postulate the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) toward that [composite], is unauthoritative, contradicted by experience, and cumbersome (*guru*).

The method of inference through the process of understanding the properties (*dharma*) conveyed by the words as they were heard, according to the manner described above, is indeed the most concise. Further details should be sought elsewhere. Thus, in cases where the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*), and so forth are composed of the meanings of their own constituent words, although the methods for establishing the corresponding inference-for-oneself (*svārthānumiti*) and inference-for-others (*parārthānumiti*) may vary due to the diversity of human intellect—given that such inferences are indeed experienced—they are nonetheless perfectly consistent. However, what remains is the consideration of the excellence of the method of exposition.

That [objection] is not applicable here, because it would result in a different type of inquiry altogether. Otherwise, since such a refutation could apply even if mere non-difference were the probandum, it would be inappropriate for you to omit stating it there and instead state it only in the case of a probandum involving "selfhood" (svatva).

If the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of "ownership" (*svatva*) and so forth, as described by you, were to constitute a refutation merely by not apprehending the underlying property (*anugata-dharma*), it would follow that the very discourse of Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others would be abolished. For instance, when a Naiyāyika says, "The mountain possesses fire," a Mīmāṃsaka might object: "Do the words 'mountain,' 'fire,' and so on, denote universals (*jāti*) or do they denote individuals (*vyakti*)? In the first case, there is sublation (*bādhā*) and other such fallacies, as well as the charge of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). In the second case, these words would be non-expressive for me. To this, only the following should be said: [the objection is invalid].

By the statement already made, the objection raised against the inference of a neutral party (*madhyastha*) and others—on the grounds that such an inference is an empirical experience—is irrelevant. All of that remains exactly the same in the present case as well.

By this, it is shown that the objections of your teachers, which proceed from a dilemma regarding the meaning of the word "self" (*sva*) within the probandum (*sādhya*) formulated by the *Nyāyāmṛta*, are indeed invalid. Furthermore, just as you provide a general definition (*anugama*) elsewhere, it can likewise be done in the present case.

To explain: the probandum (*sādhya*) consists in possessing a difference qualified by something [else], either through the relation of "possessing such an absence" (an absence whose counterpositiveness resides in itself and is delimited by the relation of being sublated by a cognition that has itself as its object), or through the relation of "inherence" (locatedness) qualified by the aforementioned possession of such an absence. Consequently, there are no faults such as the unestablished nature of the qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) or the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*). Furthermore, the objection that "there is no universal property (*anugatadharma*) in your view" has been answered;
and since it can also be stated according to the opponent's own system, everything is consistent.

As for the objection raised by some—having introduced an alternative view—that the proof of difference delimited by the time of liberation common to both those bound in fetters and those released from them constitutes a *siddhasādhanatā* (proving what is already established), and that the difference delimited by the time of supreme liberation (*paramamukti*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), and thus their refutation of the proof of difference delimited by the time of liberation is itself an unstated refutation: we have no injury whatsoever from this, so enough of this.

It is incorrect to say that it is easy to state that absence functions as a cause in the form of a "bond" (bandha) through the relation of *anuyogitā* (the property of being the locus of negation). For, if one introduces "absence-ness" (*abhāvatva*) as the delimiting property of the substratum (*dharmitāvacchedaka*), then since "absence-ness" alone would serve as the delimiting property of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*), the other part [of the definition] would be redundant. Furthermore, if that [delimiting property] were not introduced, such a cognition would be unestablished, as it would lack a delimiting property for its substratum.

Otherwise, even at the time of the sublation "the absence is not of the jar," there would arise from a sentence such as "the jar does not exist" a cognition that apprehends both the property of absence and the jar according to the principle of "two in one," because of the rule that in cases where the relation is *anuyogitā* (the property of being the locus), it is necessarily the *anuyogitā* qualified by the counter-positivehood (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by the delimiting property of the qualifier (*prakāratāvacchedaka-dharma*) that appears as the relation. Consequently, since this would entail the absolute absence of all bondage, the argument would suffer from the fallacy of the unestablished reason (*sādhanavaikalya*) in the case of one who is released from shackles.

Furthermore, if one does not accept absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) in the locus of prior non-existence of destruction, there would be the consequence of partial unestablishedness (bhāgāsiddhi) in positions other than that of God (Īśvara).

Nor can it be argued that even if bondage (*bandha*) is a cause by virtue of the relation of being the locus of its own non-connection, "bondage-ness" (*bandhatva*) is neither a universal (*jāti*) nor an impartite adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), because there is a lack of evidence for such a claim; rather, it is simply the state of being a producer of suffering (*duḥkhaprayojakatva*). To this it should not be replied that since the state of being a producer is itself the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*) through the aforementioned relation, the other part [of the definition] is redundant. For in our view, there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) to accepting the universal of bondage-ness, which is attested by the uniform cognition "this is bondage."

Furthermore, it is possible to establish that suffering (*duḥkha*) is a cause by means of the relation of "possessing a non-existence of connection whose counter-positive is that which necessitates its own origination.

Now, one might object: "Previously, under the view that accepts a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*), since it was argued that being of the nature of transmigratory existence (*saṃsārarūpatva*) cannot serve as a qualifier for suffering, how can it function as a cause? This is not so; for [suffering] functions as a cause precisely by virtue of being suffering produced by transmigratory existence (*saṃsārajanyaduḥkhatva*). The probandum (*sādhya*) must also be refined by introducing it in such a manner as: "the state of being a locus of the non-existence of a connection with suffering produced by transmigratory existence that resides in itself," and so forth.

Pervasion (*vyāpti*) must also be stated in such a manner as: "That which is related [to the probans] by way of the relation consisting in the absence of a connection whose counter-positive is the instigator of the suffering produced by that [probans]," and so forth; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

Nor should it be argued that this [etymological derivation] is unintended by the author because such a traditional relationship has not been stated anywhere by him; for in the *Tattvaprakāśikā* and other works, in the context of defining the meaning of the term "Nārāyaṇa," it is accepted as a relationship in passages such as: "The *nāras* are the Vedas; he is Nārāyaṇa because they are his 'way' (*ayana*) insofar as they are what is to be expounded; or, the *nāras* are the liberated souls; he is Nārāyaṇa because they are his 'way' insofar as they are what is to be attained.

Even though [the relationship of being the object of attainment] is not a relation that determines occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*), like the relationship of being the object of a cognition (*viṣayitā*), there is no contradiction in its being a delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*); thus, what was stated is indeed correct.

Furthermore, even for the teacher [Gaṅgeśa], it is not contradictory for the property of being blue smoke (*nīladhūmatva*) to be the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*). This is because there is no evidence for a delimitorhood of pervasion that consists in a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*), and because such a view has been refuted. Rather, it is merely technical (*pāribhāṣika*) in the sense of being "co-present with its own delimited [locus]" and so forth; and this is not contradictory in the case of *nīladhūmatva* and the like. As for the fact that the reason "because of blue smoke" (*nīladhūmāt*) is not employed in formal logic (*nyāya*), that is simply due to the speaker's defeat (*nigraha*).

When the reason is being indicated by the word "smoke" (dhūma), if one employs the qualification "blue color" (nīlarūpa) out of a desire to convey it, that [qualification] is redundant because it serves no purpose, as it conveys what was not sought after. Since such a desire cannot exist unless the speaker is under the delusion that there is a purpose for it, this constitutes a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) because it reveals the speaker’s error.

Where a single word capable of conveying the reason (*hetu*) ought to be employed, there is no distinction between stating "because of knowability" (*prameyatvāt*) and stating "because of being an object of cognition" (*viṣayatvāt*); and since there is likewise no distinction regarding the fact that what is expressed by those terms is pervaded (*vyāpyatva*), there is no defeat (*nigraha*) in such a case. Therefore, the statement of the reason "because of knowability" (*prameyatvāt*) is indeed correct. Nor should it be argued that a statement of the reason consisting of a single nominal stem—such as one intended to convey the knowledge of "smokiness" (*dhūmatva*) as delimited by the object of the knowledge of a crow's teeth—would be incorrect; for if such a word were actually present, we would simply accept the consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Nor should it be argued that if that [subject] had been previously introduced, the causal statement "therefore" (*tasmāt*) would be valid as an indicator of it; for such an application of the maxim (*nyāya*) involving the word "all" (*sarva*) is non-traditional, precisely because such usage does not occur in practice. Furthermore, in common worldly usage, such a formulation is accepted only when that subject has already been present in the mind.

It should not be argued that, in such a case, it is improper for the speaker to intend to convey a reason with a cumbersome (guru) formulation while abandoning the intention to convey a reason with a concise (laghu) formulation—thereby resulting in the speaker’s defeat (*nigraha*) on the grounds of "being a cognizable object" (*prameyatva*). This is because stating both cumbersome and concise qualifications regarding a single subject is established by tradition (*sampradāya*). Otherwise, since even the phrase "due to the prior non-existence of smoke" (*dhūma-prāgabhāvāt*) would become inadmissible, it would follow that those [prior non-existences] could not be accepted as reasons.
Furthermore, since this has been accepted by the author of the *Dīdhiti* and others, one cannot claim that such an admission is undesirable in this context.

If it is argued that just as in the case of an excess of reasons (*hetvādhikya*), a defeat is likewise appropriate when there is an excess of qualifiers of the reason (*hetuviśeṣaṇādhikya*), we reply: True. However, what is called "excess of reasons" is simply the employment of another word that conveys a different reason; for in reality, that which exists cannot be abandoned, and furthermore, it is impossible to convey two distinct properties delimiting the nature of being a reason simultaneously by means of a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Thus, while an excess of reasons is invariably a ground for defeat, an excess of qualifiers of the reason is not so.

In the employment of a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expressing a qualified object, there is an absence of the excess [of meaning] that would be occasioned by the employment of another word; for such excess only arises when [the qualification] is presented as a separate word (*pṛthakpada*). Therefore, if your intention is that it is indeed proper for there to be a distinction between [the properties of] knowability (*prameyatva*), "blue," smoke, and so forth, that too is exactly the same for me. Here too, since the stated reason is expressed by the word "liberated-ness" (*muktatva*), and because there is no occasion for a defeat (*nigraha*) consisting of excess due to the introduction of another qualification by means of another word, the statement of the stated reason is proper.

This point should be noted here: even if the state of being the locus of the absence of connection with bondage, or the state of being the locus of the absence of connection with the transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) to be described later, contains qualifying attributes that do not exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it is nonetheless proper for it to serve as a logical reason (*hetu*). This is because such attributes, by way of dispelling doubts regarding their lack of necessity (*aprayojakatā*), are useful for determining pervasion (*vyāpti*); thus, that which contains them possesses the status of being the delimiting factor of the pervaded (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*).

This is because the mere state of being a locus—whether as the locus of non-existence in general, or the locus of relational non-existence—is possible even without the aforementioned probandum (such as "prior state") and without any difference [between the two]. For it is observed that, without any difference, the state of being a locus consisting of its own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*) exists in a jar with respect to "knowability" (*prameyatva*), and the state of being a locus consisting of its own essential nature exists in the absence of the relation of a jar with respect to the jar itself; therefore, it is impossible to establish the absence of such states in the present case without assuming a difference.

Regarding the argument beginning with "the prior state" (*prāgavasthā*) and so forth, it is even more irrelevant as a probans (*sādhya*). For while the stated reason (*hetu*) may be established by accepting some kind of mere difference (*bheda-mātra*), there is no basis for accepting a difference accompanied by the aforementioned qualification.

However, if the aspect of the absence of the counter-positive—whether it be bondage or saṃsāra—is taken as a qualifier, then because the manifestation of its opposition with its own counter-positive depends on the non-existence of that opposition at the same time and in the same locus (defined as the absence of coexistence in the same locus at the same time), there arises a certainty of pervasion through the emergence of the reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*) consisting in the consequence of total annihilation, provided one does not admit a difference between the locus of the counter-positive at that time and one's own locus.

Thus, when the opponent raises the objection that the probandum need not reside in the subject (*pakṣa*) itself—thereby suggesting the reason is irrelevant (*aprayojaka*)—it is necessary to include a qualification to the reason in order to produce the favorable inference (*anukūlatarka*) that will refute this. This is because, as will be explained in the passage beginning with "of the liberated and the unliberated," such an objection cannot be refuted without a favorable inference. Furthermore, if mere difference (*bheda*) were not admitted, the distinction between the bound and the unbound would be untenable; consequently, just as the cessation of the cause of bondage (which consists in the absence of bondage and the absence of transmigratory existence) would follow, so too would the status of being the locus of non-connection (*saṃsargābhāvādhikaraṇatva*) become impossible due to the absence of its seed.

Even in the absence of difference, [the argument] is established by taking the non-existence of some thing, such as a hare's horn, at the time of the creation of a particular blade of grass and so forth. If one does not admit difference existing in the prior state, then since the destruction of difference must be accepted, there would be an attainment of identity with transmigrating beings who were previously distinct from oneself; this would result in the collapse of the distinction between the liberated and the unliberated, and thus liberation itself would be impossible. Furthermore, the favorable argument (anukūlatarka) continues to apply: that if one admits the production of another difference, it involves unnecessary complexity (gaurava).

Now, one might object: since the absence of connection with saṃsāra—consisting of its own destruction—is established through the disappearance of difference even by way of identity with present transmigrators, and since there is no usage of the term "liberated" even for a transmigrator by taking into account the absence of connection with another instance of saṃsāra (due to that absence not being the nature of liberation), it is impossible to bring about the cessation of that [saṃsāra]; therefore, the collection (*kūṭa*) of absences of connection with saṃsāra must be the probans (*hetu*).

For this very reason, since the collection of absences of transmigratory existence (saṃsārābhāvakūṭa) consisting of the absence of both [the self and transmigratory existence] can be established even without a difference [between the two], it would be non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*). Therefore, the term "conjunction" (*saṃsarga*) is meaningful for the purpose of securing the inclusion of the absence that is the opposite of the conjunction with transmigratory existence. However, the mere collection of absences (*abhāvakūṭa*) is not the probans (*hetu*), because since the destruction of another person's transmigratory existence and so forth would also be included within such a collection, it would result in the locus of such a collection being unestablished (*aprasiddha*). Rather, it is logical that the probans is the collection of absences whose respective counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are all the transmigratory existences.

Regarding the cause of the jar and so forth, there is no deficiency in the probans (sādhana) even in the case of the example, because of the aforementioned "absolute existence" (kūṭasattva). But how is it in the alternative where the absence of bondage is not intended? Even in that case, the argument is non-conclusive (aprayojaka), because the absence of some counter-correlative (pratiyogin) restricted to its own locus—specifically, a single instance of destroyed bondage—is compatible with the probandum being absent, according to the stated reasoning. For the contradiction between such an instance of bondage and its absence is not eliminated by the non-acceptance of difference; nor does the elimination of that [contradiction] follow upon the absence of the probandum in the subject (pakṣa).

If it is argued that the causal status of the aggregate of absences of bondage and contact is not tenable—because even in one released from shackles, there exists at least the bondage consisting of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), and thus, due to the absence of the aggregate of those absences, there would be a deficiency in the probans (sādhanavaikalya)—we say: no.

This is because what is intended as the reason (*hetu*) is the state of being the locus of the absence of bondage at a time when there exists an absence that is contradictory to the very absence which defines [the entity] itself. For, by introducing a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*)—namely, that if difference were non-existent in the locus of the aforementioned reason, it would result in the collapse of contradiction—the pervasion (*vyāpti*) becomes easily grasped. Furthermore, this same unfavorable consequence applies even if those two [bondage and its absence] were identical due to the destruction of a prior difference; and if one were to postulate yet another difference, there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*). This favorable argument is to be seen in other cases of the probandum (*sādhya*).

Nor should it be argued that even in this case, the qualification "having bondage as its counter-correlative" (bandhapratiyogikatva) in the absence [of difference] is redundant; for since even the locus-ness (adhikaraṇatā) of such another absence is untenable without difference, the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) is possible. This is because, if the word "bondage" (bandha) were taken to mean insentient matter (jaḍa) which causes suffering, then everything would be such, and there would be no basis for excluding pure consciousness (cinmātra); therefore, it must be admitted that the word "bondage" itself indicates the intended meaning [of being a counter-correlative of bondage].

Alternatively, if the absence were not specified by a particular counter-positive, then due to doubt regarding the nature of such an absence, there would be no immediate ascertainment of the nature of the reason as qualified by the delimitor of its causal status; consequently, the ascertainment of pervasion (vyāpti) would be impossible. Therefore, that qualification [of the counter-positive] is provided. And once that qualification is given, because the specific absence immediately flashes forth, the apprehension of pervasion indeed occurs.

Just as when the absence of the generality of conjunction (*saṃyoga-sāmānyābhāva*) is to be proven by means of inherence (*samavāya*), one introduces the property of being delimited by the relation of inherence into the absences of all particular conjunctions (*saṃyogīya-yāvad-viśeṣābhāva*); thus, in the body of the universal pervasion (*sāmānyamukha-vyāpti*), the property of having inherence as its delimiting relation (*samavāyāvacchinna-pratiyogikatva*) is introduced into the scope of the probans (*hetu*).

Otherwise, although there would be no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the mere collection of individual absences (*viśeṣābhāvakūṭamātra*) from the general absence whose counter-positiveness is delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāyasambandhāvacchinnapratiyogitāka*), a determination of pervasion (*vyāpti*) would still be impossible due to the doubt that the mere collection of individual absences might not reside in any locus whatsoever; this is the case here as well. And this is clear in Gadādhara’s *Siddhāntalakṣaṇagadādharī*. The term "relation" (*saṃsarga*) is used to ensure that opposition (*virodha*) is understood as being constituted by a specific relation.

When [liberation] is established as the alternative, such a cause would be either the destruction of saṃsāra or its absolute non-existence. This is because even the destruction of saṃsāra residing in one person possesses a contradiction—defined as the absence of co-occurrence in a single substratum—with the saṃsāra existing in another person.

The meaningfulness of a qualifier—even one that does not preclude deviation (vyabhicāra)—but is useful for the ascertainment of pervasion (vyāpti), was demonstrated by Yādavācārya in his *Saudhasamayacaraṇa-ṭippaṇī* through its role in eliminating "establishment otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhi*) in the inference: "An atom possesses ten parts, because of its simultaneous conjunction with the ten directions. This has likewise been demonstrated in both the *Gurvadvaitacandrikā* and the *Laghuadvaitacandrikā* during the refutation of inferences intended to prove reality (*satyatā*).

In the *tarka* (reductio) formulated by Gadādhara in his *Tarkagrantha*: "If smoke were [1] not the counter-correlate of a generativity residing in fire as delimited by a relation other than conjunction, and [2] were devoid of being the producedness as determined by fire as delimited by a relation other than conjunction, while [3] being devoid of the producedness counter-correlated to a generativity residing in fire as delimited by the relation of conjunction, then smoke would not be produced by fire"—in this *tarka*, the first conjunctive clause (*satyantam*) of the *āpādaka* (the antecedent condition), although it does not exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*), is nevertheless useful for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Having explained its purposefulness, the consensus of the Miśras is stated: "The authors of the treatises also maintain that if a qualification is added to the example, there is a deficiency in either the probandum or the probans;
if one [of the two] is unestablished, it is redundant; but if both are unestablished, it is simply a case of the non-establishment of the qualified."

Thus, on the occasion of the commentary (*anuvyākhyā*) on the "Chapter on Devotion" (*bhaktipādīya*), it was stated that a qualification which is not conducive to the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed redundant; this was not said merely because it does not exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Therefore, this [point] is not extraordinary.

Thus, although the qualification serves a purpose according to the manner stated, one should understand that the provision of an answer by way of a *pratibandi* (reductio ad absurdum) is intended either because the resolution of this very point can be easily grasped by the students themselves through the very same method—following the favorable arguments (*anukūlatarka*) to be presented in the root text—or else to demonstrate to the opponent that such an objection is improper once he himself has employed the probans "because of being an object of knowledge" (*prameyatvāt*), or for the sake of making the resolution easy.

Therefore, it is improper to place exclusive reliance solely on the opponent's position. For even you yourself, in the *Anuvyākhyāna-vyākhyā*, have admitted that a redundant qualification (*vyartha-viśeṣaṇa*) results in the fallacy of the unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*). Furthermore, when that [redundancy] constitutes a defect only by its very excess in the opponent's view, then to place exclusive reliance on that view alone would result in abandoning your own doctrine and thus entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

Although that term was explained as "or else" (*atha vā*) by way of providing an additional [qualification], it was nonetheless done without abandoning the previous alternative. Otherwise, since an option regarding a real entity is impossible, it would follow that the previous alternative is rooted in error. Furthermore, it is improper to explain it according to another's system when one is in the process of defining one's own view; for it is not correct to say that there is a failure to establish pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) simply because a qualification other than those included within that [previous] alone is introduced by another word.

If that were the case, then for the very same "blue smoke," there would arise at one and the same time the contradictory properties of being pervaded and not being pervaded, resulting from the two words "from blue smoke" and "therefore" being uttered by different persons with different intentions. Nor should it be argued that the status of being a fault is settled because it is constituted by specific persons and times; for it is precisely ignorance, non-establishment, and so forth, that possess such a nature.

The [objection] that "since this [reason] falls under the contradiction of the reason (*hetuvirodha*) in the form of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) within the view that it is unestablished due to lack of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), it must be stated that such a meaning is defective for that person [who holds the view], yet there is no restrictive rule that such a meaning is non-defective for another person" is thus refuted.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that—having raised the objection that a refutation based on conceptualizing a specific form after a general form has been employed later would lead to an over-extension (atiprasañjakatva)—the statement that the aforementioned conceptualization is the "seed" [of the fault] because there is no consensus regarding the general form would be contradicted. For even if the general form exists, the aforementioned sequence of conceptualizations and the faults of those positions resulting from the introduction of qualifiers that exclude the objects of error remain applicable. This is because, first of all, "dṛśyatvatva" (the property of being perceivability) does not serve as the delimitor of the reason (*hetutāvacchedaka*).

If, according to your own view, you take "being perceivable" (*dṛśyatva*) as it is erroneously attributed to the Self (*ātman*), then a fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) arises; therefore, with the intention that you must state a definition of the probans (*hetutāvacchedaka*) that excludes such cases, [the opponent says]: "If [you mean] the property of being perceivable as qualified by 'indefinability' (*anirvācyatva*) in the form of empirical existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*), then that is unestablished (*asiddha*) for me."

If, when the objection is raised that "that [reason] which incorporates ultimate reality is unestablished," one were to suspect—on the grounds that a certain generality existing in both our intended empirical reality (which is indefinable) and your intended ultimate reality, yet excluded from what is apprehended through error, could serve as the delimiting condition for the probans (*hetutāvacchedaka*), and that by this much the possibility of avoiding either "unestablishedness" (*anyatarāsiddhi*) or "inconstancy" (*vyabhicāra*) would arise, making your alternative analysis irrelevant—it is replied: "ultimate reality..."

Having accepted that the conventional (vyāvahārika) is understood through words that are conventionally false (mithyā) by another synonym, it is precisely my own position that there is no single universal (*sāmānya*) common to both [the real and the conventional]. You yourself have admitted that "the state of being perceivable" (*dṛśyatvatva*) is the delimiting factor of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Therefore, with the intention that such an alternative is indeed logical, the refutation of such a universal is entirely appropriate; hence, there is no fault whatsoever.

One must necessarily state his intention in this very way: otherwise, since you have accepted that the world is indeed perceptible (*dṛśyatva*), it must be either real or false. In that case, the property of perceptibility has certainly been accepted by you; and you should not maintain that it subsists in both the false and the real. Thus, if he intends for "perceptibility" alone—setting aside the addition of qualifiers such as "indefinability" (*anirvacanīyatva*) or "reality"—to serve as the logical reason (*hetu*), then the aforementioned dilemma is entirely irrelevant.

Otherwise, there would arise the undesirable consequence that for both the Mīmāṃsaka and the Naiyāyika, it would be impossible to take phonemes (*varṇa*) as the subject (*pakṣa*) in order to establish their respective positions regarding the eternity or non-eternity of sound. For the Mīmāṃsakas, a phoneme is asserted to be a substance (*dravya*), whereas by the Naiyāyikas, it is asserted to be a quality (*guṇa*). Furthermore, neither of them accepts that the common property (*sāmānyadharma*) of "phonemeness" (*varṇatva*) exists in a phoneme that is of the nature of a substance or in one that is of the nature of a quality.

And thus, if one party takes "color" (varṇa) as the subject (pakṣa) while the other takes "color as a substance" (dravyātmakavarṇa) as the subject, there arises the fault that my own position is unestablished; yet if "color as a quality" (guṇātmakavarṇa) is taken as the subject, your position is unestablished. Since such objections would follow, the aforementioned intention is indeed appropriate.

Nor should it be argued that even in the case of the reason "because of smoke," since a qualifying attribute must necessarily be included there to exclude fallacious appearances (*ābhāsa*) and avoid deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the objection of "unestablished for one or both parties" (*anyatarāsiddhi*) and other such defects is possible there as well; therefore, agreement [on the definition] in that case is improper. For, according to the reasoning already stated, such a defect exists everywhere even in the opponent's view. However, when considering two parties who both accept the universal "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*), the agreement mentioned there is intended only to show that one should not engage in such conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) as "being connected to this particular place" and so forth. Enough of this digression; let us return to the subject at hand.

Now, if the meaning is "being the counter-positive of absolute non-existence," then since that [non-existence] is the meaning of the particle, it would be construed as the locus (*āśrayatā*) with respect to the referent of the co-occurring word "silver" (*rajata*); thus, the resulting meaning would be "silver is the counter-positive of absolute non-existence. But how could there be a cognition where absolute non-existence is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)? Even if one were to accept—due to the diversity of linguistic convention—that the referent of the co-occurring word "silver" and so forth is construed as being the counter-positive through the relation of subsistence (*ādheyatā*), there would still only be a cognition where the counter-positiveness is the qualificand, not one where the non-existence is the qualificand.

Because it is included within the scope of the delimitor of the denotable object (*vācyatāvacchedaka*) of that [term]. Furthermore, it is undisputed that the words *asat*, *tuccha*, *alīka*, and *mithyā* are synonyms. If these also had as their meaning the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), then it would be untenable for the word *mithyā*, being a synonym for them, to have the meaning of being the counter-correlate of absolute non-existence. Alternatively, if they too had the meaning of being the counter-correlate of absolute non-existence, then the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the horn of a hare is false" (*śaśaviṣāṇam alīkam*) would be untenable.

Because "mithyā" is an indeclinable (avyaya), even though it may be construed with a difference [as a qualifier] there, it cannot be so construed here as it was there; for its construction with non-difference is sublated. Furthermore, this would lead to the absurd consequence of such usage as "the horn of a hare is mithyā" or "the horn of a hare is false" (alīka), since the meanings of the genitive or locative case—namely, relation and the state of being contained—would be possible within the meaning of the words "mithyā" and "alīka" as previously stated. Nor is the referent of words such as "mithyā" and "alīka" merely that which is the counter-positive of absolute non-existence.

It should not be argued that the referents of words such as "hare's horn," when uttered together [with other words], are connected only through non-difference; for if there were a doubt regarding the non-existence of the denoted object, and one had to state its very existence, it would follow that the statement "because of the existence of non-existence characterized as being the counter-positive of absolute non-existence" would be redundant, as it would merely be stating the existence of that which is already denoted. Nor should it be argued that even this [non-existence] must be denoted as a qualifier; for in our established doctrine (siddhānta), while the status of being the ground for the application of a word (vṛttinimittatā) is accepted for a qualifier, the presence of a primary denotative power (śakti) is not admitted. If this is said, we reply: no.

The inherent capacity of a word to produce a cognition possessing a particular objective content (*viṣayitā*) is precisely what is called its "power" (*śakti*). And this power is useful only when it is known. All things that serve as the determinants (*nirūpaka*) of such objective content are indeed "denotable" (*śakya*). For this very reason, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is also power with respect to the syntactic relation (*anvaya*). If one were to admit the appearance of something non-denotable in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), then—just as in the case of the "ground for application" (*pravṛttinimitta*)—the relation itself could likewise appear [without being denoted]. Consequently, it would follow that it is useless to admit power with respect to "that which is related to what is other than the incapable" (*yogyetarānvita*).

However, the knowledge of the expressive power (*śakti*) conducive to verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) takes the form "the jar-ness-qualified [entity] is denotable by the word 'jar'," and not the form "jar-ness and the jar are both denotable by the word 'jar'. Therefore, because [the property of being the jar] is not the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the portion of the power that constitutes the object of the knowledge conducive to verbal cognition, there is the conventional usage of "non-denotability" (*aśakyatva*) regarding it. And thus, since denotability exists as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the portion consisting of not being the counter-correlative (*apratiyogitva*) of such [absence], the aforementioned commentary (*ṭīkā*) is indeed consistent.

Nor does it follow that if the words "false" (*mithyā*) and so forth have as their referent the negation of what has been stated, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition, "That which is denoted by the word 'false' does not exist. This is because such a cognition—namely, "There is no general denotable object"—is sublated by the existence of the denotable object in the form of having that [stated] thing as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). For this very reason, it was stated that the denotable object, in the form of having that as its counter-correlative, exists. However, the cognition, "That which is denotable as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) does not exist," is indeed accepted. Nor should it be asked, "How can that which is non-existent be denotable?"

For there is no contradiction in the presence therein of the aforementioned "denotability," which consists in not being the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of a subjecthood (*viṣayitā*). Furthermore, even in the *arthavat-sūtra*, what is intended by "possessing meaning" (*arthavattva*) is precisely the state of possessing a denotative power (*śaktimat*), and not the capacity to generate a cognition having an existent (*sat*) as its qualificandum. Were it otherwise, it would follow that words such as "non-existent" (*alīka*) would lose their status as words (*padatva*).

However, having accepted that the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the word *mithyā* and its absence (*abhāva*) are indeed distinct meanings, and having accepted the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the meaning of the co-occurring word with the counter-correlate as being through identity (*abheda*), the cognition characterized by the predominance of the absence is admitted in the case of the word *mithyā* precisely on the basis of experience. As for the statement that the words *mithyā* and *alīka* are synonyms, this is because their meanings are not significantly different. If it is argued that the cognition in which the absence is predominant is shown only as a subsequent [stage], then there is no fault whatsoever.

The proponents of illusion (māyāvādins), however, maintain that the non-existent is "devoid of designation" (*nirupākhya*) and "not an object of the power of words," thereby asserting that the non-existent lies beyond the scope of linguistic capacity. This is not tenable; for it would follow that words such as *alīka* ("unreal") themselves would lack a referent. Nor can it be argued that these words denote the "indescribable" (*anirvacanīya*), because this would result in the rejection of the validity of the sentence "A rabbit’s horn is unreal," which is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by all schools of thought. Furthermore, one cannot argue that this sentence merely generates a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and thus does not possess validity as defined by its capacity to produce cognition, for such a position is not my own consensus.

Since even conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not arise in a person who lacks knowledge of the relationship between words and their referents, it is necessary—even for that purpose—to admit the apprehension of the word-potency (*śakti-graha*) for unreal words such as "non-existent" (*alīka*). If one were to accept that the unreal appears through the cognition of potency in something indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), it would follow that a cloth could appear through the cognition of potency in a jar. Other points will be refuted further below. For the Naiyāyikas and others who do not accept the cognition of the non-existent, the contradiction of the status of words like "unreal" as being actual words is quite evident.
Any attempt to somehow imagine them as having a real referent is contrary to experience; therefore, we desist.

However, for one who maintains that absolute non-existence has an unreal counter-positive (*aprāmāṇika-pratiyogika*), a sentence such as "the jar does not exist on this floor," where there is no connection whatsoever with a jar on that floor, conveys the absolute non-existence whose counter-positive is the jar qualified by subsistence in that floor; it does not [convey] "the absence of a jar on this floor. At that time, even the perception expressed by that sentence would have that very same form. This is because there is no deficiency even if the subsistence in the floor does not appear within the aspect of non-existence in that cognition.

In the case of perception, after the recollection of a jar and the subsequent appearance of the jar as residing on the ground, there is the appearance of the non-existence of that very [jar]—though it is non-existent—in its qualified form within the aspect of negation (*abhāvāṃśa*). Nor is there an inconsistency in the appearance of a negation whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the object of such a cognition, even though the cognition serving as the cause is not induced (*anāhārya*). This is because, according to this view, such a cognition is the very thing that constitutes the contradiction here. Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even one who has ascertained "there is a jar on the ground" through a statement or similar means could still have a cognition of such a negation.

It should not be argued that if the knowledge serving as the cause [of the erroneous cognition] is itself "artificial" (*āhārya*), then there must be a requirement for a further apprehension of sublation (*bādhagraha*) regarding that, and for that too another artificial apprehension, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This is because the causal knowledge in the form "the jar exists on the ground" does not involve the awareness of its own existence [as a false object], and thus lacks the capacity to act as an obstacle (*pratibandhaka*). Only a cognition that involves the awareness of existence can function as an obstructor or as something to be obstructed. Furthermore, since such a cognition is not artificial, it does not require another apprehension of sublation, and therefore no infinite regress occurs.

Now, is cognition that does not apprehend existence an error (*bhrama*) or a valid cognition (*pramā*)? We say it is indeed a valid cognition. Nor should it be asked: "How can that which has a qualifier (*prakāra*) in a locus where that [qualifier] is absent be called a valid cognition? For we accept that only a cognition—which, having understood the meaning of an opponent's statement whose absence is ascertained by oneself, is treated as an error by a restater (*anuvādaka*), and thus falls outside the scope of the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) of a discerning person—is an error, precisely because it is treated as having a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) through its apprehension of existence therein. For this very reason, it was said by the Teachers:

"Because error consists precisely in a cognition otherwise—that is, the apprehension of the non-existent as existent and the existent as non-existent. Nor should it be argued that in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), since the cognizer’s knowledge is an "induced error" (*āhāryabhrama*)—having arisen intentionally based on their own prior understanding—it does not fall within the scope of the conventional usage of "error" when that [prior knowledge] is taken into account.

Because one who intentionally performs a distortion of their own limbs falls within the scope of the conventional usage "one with distorted limbs," it follows all the more that when one intentionally produces an error, it is impossible to avoid falling within the scope of the conventional usage "one who is deluded. Furthermore, since we observe that in cases such as [the perception of] a post (yogya) which is cognized as being free from defects, the cognition is merely reiterative (anuvādaka), it is untenable for that cognition to be an error, as it is not produced by a defect.

For this very reason, the view that only the desire which prompts that [erroneous] cognition constitutes the defect (*doṣa*) therein is refuted. This is because, in those respective cases, there is no basis for postulating a delusion or its causal defect without the evidence consisting of the conventional usage of terms such as "being mistaken. Otherwise, one would face the consequence of an infinite number of specific instances—such as the conjunctions with air at that time residing in that person—acting as causes by way of being defects due to their co-location, resulting in a lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) and the onset of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Nor should it be argued that the fault (doṣa) is to be postulated as the very desire (icchā) known to produce that cognition, and not as the conjunction with air (vāyu-saṃyoga), because the latter's status as a producer has not been established. For, since the distinct causal role of desire as a fault has not been established, the lack of a decisive argument (vinigamakābhāva) remains firm; furthermore, since the lack of a decisive argument is unavoidable when considering those factors already established as causes of that cognition—namely, the specific moment, the unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa), and the contact (sannikarṣa)—the fault would remain unaccounted for. Moreover, if its being an error were accepted while maintaining that it is not produced by a fault, then that [definition of error] would become merely conventional (pāribhāṣika).

Nor should it be argued that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is also absent because [this cognition] does not determine the object; for since only a valid cognition that apprehends existence (*sattva*) is determinative of the object, even if this [cognition] does not determine the object due to its not apprehending existence, its status as valid is established for our opponents simply by virtue of its being distinct from error, just as in the case of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*). Nor can it be argued that its validity is impossible because its definition is "valid cognition is knowledge that accords with reality" (*yathārtha-jñānam pramā*), and this [cognition] is non-accordant with reality (*ayathārtha*).

It should not be argued that even if the term "valid cognition" (*pramā*) is used figuratively for a cognition merely because it is distinct from error, this would lead to the acceptance of a type of knowledge distinct from doubt, misconception, and valid cognition, thereby resulting in a deviation from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*). This is because the "truthfulness" (*yathārthatva*) of valid cognition does not consist in its having a non-existent object as its content; for if it did, the definition would fail to apply to the valid cognition, "The horn of a hare is non-existent. Rather, truthfulness consists precisely in being distinct from error. Furthermore, since the word "valid cognition" (*pramā*) occurring in the taxonomic statement (*vibhājakavākya*) also refers to that same [distinction from error], there is no deviation from established tenets.

Nor should it be argued that this cognition is impossible because, given its eternity, it would be indifferent toward the cognition of whether something is an existent or a non-existent, and thus such a cognition could not arise.

Since the intrinsic validity (*prāmāṇya-svatastva*) of that [cognition] is its default state, it is accepted that the causal complex for grasping non-existence (*asattva*) within that [validity] is opposed by virtue of occurring at the time of the effect; thus, in the very second moment, the cognition of non-existence—in the form of being the counter-positive of negation—arises. Consequently, the moment constituting the locus of that aforementioned cognition is not the locus of the causal complex for grasping existence. Nor does it follow that, even in the absence of the grasp of existence, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the manifestation of non-existence in that [locus] at the very moment the aforementioned cognition arises.

It cannot be argued that this contradicts the statements of the ancients—namely, that the aforementioned cognition is not an error despite being described as having superimposition as its cause, and that the doubt which serves as the occasion for the Yogin’s question is "artificial" (*āhārya*)—because such a cognition is a specific kind of error. For it is consistent with those statements, since it does not apprehend existence (*sattva*) and is therefore not obstructed by contrary cognitions. This is because it is not apprehended solely by the causal complex that produces knowledge of existence, and thus its initial apprehension is impossible without the causal complex that apprehends non-existence. Nor does it contradict the claim that the aforementioned cognition is not an error, nor the claim regarding the artificiality of the doubt, because [the latter] is a specific type of error. This is because, by not apprehending existence and by not being obstructed by contrary cognitions, those statements remain coherent.

Furthermore, the cognition "there is no existence in a rabbit’s horn" must be said to be preceded by a knowledge of existence in the rabbit’s horn; likewise, the cognition "there is no non-existence in a jar" must be said to be preceded by a knowledge of non-existence in the jar. And thus, for those possessing such cognitions of negation, there would follow the undesirable consequence of their being objects of erroneous worldly discourse, because the non-existent rabbit’s horn and the like are perceived as existent, and the existent jar and the like are perceived as non-existent.

In that regard, even with respect to the aspect of the appearing existence, there is the apprehension of existence; thus, in the refinement of the definition of error, the same previously mentioned defect arises by taking as the cause of the cognition the cognition that "existence does not exist in the existence of the silver in the mother-of-pearl."

In that regard, even though existence (*sattva*) is manifest, if one introduces the property of "pervading other existents" into the definition (*pariṣkāra*), then—in order to avoid the aforementioned defects by taking as the cause of the cognition that negates existence in various instances the cognition that serves as its cause—one must likewise introduce such refinements in subsequent cases as well. Consequently, it would follow that there is an infinite regress regarding the object-determination (*viṣayatā*) in error, and that the nature of error (*bhramatva*) defined by that [object-determination] would become impossible to apprehend. This need not be asserted, because in the case of a jar or the like, where existence is manifested, existence manifests itself in its own part (*svāṃśa*) by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

That very cognition contradicts a cognition that apprehends non-existence with respect to the aspect of the jar and the aspect of existence. It generates various types of linguistic usage, such as "the jar exists," "the existence of that [jar] exists," and "the existence of that [existence] exists," and so forth. Likewise, even in the cognition "the horn of a rabbit is non-existent," existence is indeed cognized with respect to non-existence; for the general causal complex of cognition is invariably restricted by the absence of any exception to its capacity to apprehend existence.

In that case, regarding the existence (*sattva*) that is appearing, existence itself appears by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*). Therefore, there is no possibility of doubt or error regarding non-existence (*asattva*) in that regard. Just as the mere cognition of the locus of the absence of a jar—namely, the absence of the jar itself—accounts for such linguistic usages as "the absence of the jar exists in the absence of the jar" or "the jar does not exist in the absence of the jar which resides in the absence of the jar," so too, the existence that consists in the general absence of sublation throughout the three periods of time accounts for the linguistic usage "existence exists in existence" and "existence exists in that existence" within the cognition that apprehends its own part.

Thus, its capacity to account for linguistic conventions such as "it exists" (sattvam) and so forth is established. Similarly, according to the view that the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) among the six categories (dravya, etc. constitutes the nature of non-existence (*abhāvatva*), it must be admitted that in cognitions such as "the jar does not exist" or "there is the absence of the jar," the nature of non-existence—which is the mutual absence of the six categories appearing within that absence—appears by its very own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

Otherwise, if such [an object] were to appear as possessing mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), then since the nature of absence (*abhāvatva*) would not be included within that body [of the cognition], there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress regarding the objects [of cognition], and it would result in the impossibility of apprehending an absence as an absence. Likewise, the appearance of existence (*sattva*), which consists in the absence of sublation (*bādhyatva*), in its own part as its own essential form (*svarūpataḥ*) is not contradictory.

And thus, regarding the definition of error as "the apprehension of non-existence as existence," there is the inclusion of a subject-predicate relation (*viṣayatā*) residing in non-existence, which is determined by a subject-predicate relation of existence that is, in turn, determined by an undelimited subject-predicate relation of itself; and [there is the inclusion] of a subject-predicate relation residing in existence, which is determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) consisting of a subject-predicate relation of non-existence that is determined by a subject-predicate relation of existence, which is itself determined by a subject-predicate relation of itself in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

Nor should it be argued that, since in the case of the error "this is silver," the silver—which is non-existent—is devoid of its own nature because even the appearance of existence therein is non-existent, how can there be an appearance of its own nature within its own part? For, since the causal complex that manifests the existence residing in the substrate (such as mother-of-pearl) is present, we accept that in the error, such as the silver, it is merely the relation to that [existence] which is superimposed; thus, existence itself is not non-existent.

Alternatively, just as even in the absence of silver and so forth, a specific objectivity (*viṣayatā*) is accepted in error—which, by the force of the causal complex of error, brings about the linguistic usage "this is silver"—so too, by that very force, a specific objectivity is accepted in valid cognition (*pramā*), which brings about the linguistic usages "silver exists" and "that existence exists," just as it does in valid cognition. Since that same [objectivity] is included in the definition of error, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. More will be said on this later.

And thus, since it is not admitted that the aforementioned cognition—in the form of a superimposition (āropa) of the counter-positive (pratiyogin), which serves as the cause for the negation "there is no existence in the silver of the mother-of-pearl" and "there is no non-existence in the jar"—has unconditioned existence (niravacchinna-sattva) as its object, there is no consequence of its being an error (bhrama).

As for the regulating factor (niyāmaka) regarding the absence of such an objective content in that cognition, subtle observers should understand, as previously stated, that it consists in the capacity of the causal complex (sāmagrī) cognizing the negation of that entity to act as an inhibitor (pratibandhaka) against a cognition possessing such an objective content, according to the circumstances. This is the direction [of the argument].

And thus, in the case of "There is no jar on the ground," both in the initial perception and in verbal cognition, the form is everywhere simply "an absolute absence whose counter-positive is a jar residing on the ground. Immediately thereafter, there arises a second cognition: "The ground possesses the absence of a jar. In that case, because one accepts a conventional (nirūḍha) secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of words such as "jar" in the sense of a jar residing on the ground, the form of the verbal cognition is "the ground possesses the absence of a jar residing on the ground."

The perceptual [cognition] has precisely the form: "the ground possesses the absence of a jar. In cases such as "there is no jar on the ground," first of all, there is known either the absence of a jar residing on the ground, or the absence of existence (sattā) whose agent is the jar having the ground as its locus. However, in the case of "there is here the absence of a jar," because there is absolute non-difference between the jar and the existence whose agent is that jar, it is understood as being the absence of such a jar.

Wherever on a surface a jar will arise or has perished, the perceptual cognition that "the jar does not exist on that surface" apprehends either the destruction or the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of the jar as related to that surface, or the destruction or prior non-existence of the relation itself as related to that surface. In the case of the prior non-existence or destruction of the relation, it is accepted that the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is the related object.

In the view that accepts the production and destruction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), there is no fault even if there is an absence of the prior non-existence and destruction having as their counter-positive a jar qualified by its connection with the ground—as in the case "there is no jar here on this ground"—because it would be cumbersome to accept those two separately, and because in the system that accepts both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*) for the sake of the identity between the blue [quality] and the jar qualified by it, there is no obstacle to accepting that the very difference having blue as its counter-positive possesses the status of having the jar qualified by blue as its counter-positive in the aforementioned instance. And thus, even if the prior non-existence and destruction having as their counter-positive a jar qualified by its connection with the ground are absent, there is no deficiency.

In cases such as "There is no jar on the ground," however, what appears is either the destruction or the prior non-existence of the existence—which is of the nature of a relation—subsisting in the jar that has the ground as its locus. But if one accepts that the meaning of the verb (the finite suffix) appears as the delimitor of the modehood (prakāratā) of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), then those two (destruction and prior non-existence) appear as belonging to the jar itself as qualified by such existence.

In the case of the cognition "Now there is no jar on this ground," what appears is simply an absolute absence whose counter-positive is unestablished (aprāmāṇika), because the jar—qualified by its being connected with this ground as delimited by this time—is non-existent. According to this view, the counter-positiveness (pratiyogitā) consists either in the objecthood (viṣayatva) that serves as the qualifier (prakāratā) determined by the objecthood that is the basis for the mention of the negative particle (nañ), or merely in the objecthood that is co-located (samānādhikaraṇa) with that [qualifier]. However, such conditions as not being the cause of the qualifierhood delimited by the relation of "residing-in" (ādheyatā-saṃsarga) need not be included.

Since it is not accepted that the locus (adhikaraṇa) appears as a non-existent element in the first cognition, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) in that case. By accepting that the second cognition necessarily arises in the form "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," all such phenomena—including the non-arising of doubt regarding that locus—are rendered intelligible.

However, some maintain that perceptual and verbal cognitions such as "there is no jar on the ground" or "there is no jar on the ground" occur precisely in the manner described in the previous system. But they do not require a superimposition (āropa) of the form "there is a jar on the ground" or "there is a jar on the ground" as the causal cognition. This is because neither the author of the root text nor the venerable commentator has stated anywhere that such a cognition serves as its cause, and because [positing it] would be irrational. Furthermore, any mention of this in certain commentaries (*ṭippaṇī*) and similar works is merely according to another school of thought and is not definitive.

Through the very presentation of the jar, the ground, and so forth without [mutual] restriction, there arises a cognition in such forms as "the absence whose counter-positive is a jar residing on the ground" or "the absence of existence having a jar as its agent and the ground as its locus. Even by that much, since the unestablished (aprāmāṇika) qualified entity appears within the aspect of the absence, the fact that the absence has an unestablished counter-positive is established.

If it is objected: "In that case, since the unestablished is negated precisely within the cognition of the absence, how can the definition of counter-positiveness stated here be possible in that context? We reply: No.

Since it is contrary to experience for any property other than that [negation] to appear in a cognition that apprehends negation, and since existence and so forth do not appear when there is a cognition explicitly mentioning the negative particle (*nañ*) regarding the aspect of absence, a doubt regarding the subsistence of existence in a particular locus cannot arise; therefore, in order to account for this established experience, one must necessarily admit a subsequent cognition apprehending existence and so forth in the second moment following that [initial cognition].

And thus, since after the cognition "there is no jar on the ground" there necessarily arises a second cognition of absence—of the form "the ground possesses the absence of a jar residing on the ground"—and this must be designated by the term 'cognition of absence', the definition applies to that [first] cognition, "there is no jar on the ground," because its objectivity (viṣayatā) exists in a qualified manner within the [ground], which is not [itself] unestablished.

In the expression "the state of being an object of a cognition that is useful for the cognition of absence," the phrase "useful for the cognition of absence" serves as a qualifier for the first cognition that is useful for the second cognition. Thus, counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) is simply the state of being an object that necessitates the mention of the negative particle (*nañ*).

In that context, in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) based on the objective state of non-existence (*abhāvatva*)—which is itself determined by the objective state of negation (*niṣedhatva*) that serves as the motivator for the mention of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the previous cognition—the word "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is indeed meaningful; it either signifies "being distinct from that" or signifies "having the nature of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) determined by an objective state residing in non-existence. Furthermore, whether such an objective state constitutes the relation (*saṃsarga*) of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*), or whether it constitutes the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the term "counter-correlate," the entire previously mentioned method of analysis should be followed.

By this, the frequent usage of the term "counter-positive" (*pratiyogitva*) in the scriptures even with respect to jars and other objects that are established as real for the Easterners (Prācīnas) is also shown to be non-faulty. Since such usage—though secondary—is possible by taking the primary counter-positiveness in the form of a "subject-object relation" (*viṣayatā*) belonging to the unstructured cognition "jar," which generates the initial cognition "there is no jar on the ground," just as one speaks of a "sonship" in a brother's son [by metaphorical extension], the word "specific" (*viśeṣa*) is included to exclude such usage in cases like the bare ground itself.

It serves the purpose of [denoting] "otherness" and so forth. Nor should it be argued that there is no basis for employing figurative usage (*gauṇavyavahāra*) regarding the ground and such; for the desire [of the speaker] itself is the regulating factor, and because, according to the maxim *ārope sati*, the aforementioned doubt is simply untenable.
