And thus, since for the production of the cognitions "there is no existence in the silver of the mother-of-pearl" and "there is no non-existence in the jar," there is no prior requirement for the cognitions "existence in the silver of the mother-of-pearl" and "non-existence in the jar," it does not follow that one who possesses those [first] cognitions is erroneous according to our view. This is because the nature of error consists precisely in the apprehension of the existent as non-existent or the non-existent as existent, where such apprehension occurs without being a qualifier (*aprakāratayā*) regarding the negative aspect (*niṣedhāṃśe*).

Nor can it be argued that the cognition of the absence of a jar—qualified by the property of being a jar and having as its counter-positive (pratiyogitā) that which resides on the ground—is impossible through a disconnected cognition (viśṛṅkhala-jñāna) of the ground and the jar, because the cause consisting of the cognition of the counter-positive qualified by the delimitor of counter-positiveness (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) would be absent. Otherwise, there would result the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of the cognition "the fire of the kitchen does not exist" following the disconnected cognition "fire and [the fire] of the kitchen," and the cognition "the jar does not exist" following the indeterminate cognition (nirvikalpaka) of a jar. This is what must be said.

Since the procedure regarding the delimitation of counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) and so forth—following the manner about to be described—is unauthenticated, the aforementioned rule is unestablished. Furthermore, because the cognition "There is no kitchen-fire at all" cannot be denied even for those who possess the certainty that "Fire is not from the kitchen," it follows that in the cognition of an absence, the knowledge of the counterpositive need not necessarily be preceded by the presentation of a property appearing either directly or indirectly in the aspect of the counterpositive.

You accept that, following the unrestricted cognition "Fire is [present] in the kitchen," for those who fail to grasp the non-relation [between the two], the cognition "Kitchen-fire does not exist" arises through the emergence of the cognition "Fire is [present] in the kitchen" at the third moment. I, however, accept that the cognition "Kitchen-fire does not exist" arises at the very second moment; for the delay of a single moment must be determined by oath, and because there is the parsimony resulting from not postulating such an intermediate cognition.

However, they say that even in a case where, following an unrestricted cognition such as "the kitchen-fire," there is the possibility of another cognition "the kitchen-fire," the non-arising of the experience-confirmed cognition "the kitchen-fire does not exist" is accounted for by the very same factor upon whose strength you establish [your position]; it is established by me as well. By this same method, the objection that the cognition "the jar does not exist" would arise immediately after the indeterminate perception (nirvikalpaka) of a jar is also refuted; furthermore, in our own system (siddhānta), there is no such thing as indeterminate perception. Thus they say.

Now, one might object: "Why is it not accepted that, just as the cognition 'the horn of a hare does not exist' involves an absence whose counter-positive is non-existent, the cognition 'there is no jar on this ground' involves an absence whose counter-positive is a jar established by valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika), and this absence is cognized as residing in the ground? Furthermore, the commentarial passages found here and there—which appear to be governed by the rule that the counter-positive must be non-existent—can somehow be interpreted [to fit this view], so there is no contradiction with them either."

Furthermore, the quality of being absolute (*ātyantikatva*) is not understood from the term "absolute non-existence" (*atyantābhāva*) itself; rather, absoluteness consists precisely in the absence of spatial and temporal limitations. Consequently, if absolute non-existence were to have an existent counter-positive (*sat-pratiyogika*), then because non-existence is in contradiction with its counter-positive, it would follow that it does not occur in the location where the counter-positive resides. This would entail a spatial limitation, thereby destroying its absoluteness. Therefore, one must accept the rule that [absolute non-existence] has only a non-existent counter-positive (*asat-pratiyogika*).

Having raised the objection that the definition of "faultlessness" (nirdoṣatva)—defined as the absolute non-existence of faults—would over-apply (ativyāpti) even to living beings who possess faults, because such beings also possess the absolute non-existence of unestablished (aprāmāṇika) faults just as the Blessed One does, the Vaṃśapallyācāryas resolved this over-extension by accepting that even a non-existence whose counter-positive (pratiyogin) is unestablished has spatial limitation, based on the passage beginning: "Because there is a contradiction between non-existence and its counter-positive, even when that counter-positive is superposed. The Ācāryas [of our own school] likewise [resolved the issue] by stating "by way of prior, posterior, and eternal existence," and "by way of prior, posterior, and eternal existence."

If it is argued that this is not so—because it has been stated that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) merely lacks a temporal limit, and since the absence of spatial restriction is not the meaning of the term "absolute," it is impossible to accept the rule that its counter-positive must be unreal in order to establish that [spatial restriction] due to the lack of any other supporting argument—we say no. For it is generally accepted that non-existences are in opposition to their own counter-positives. And this opposition does not consist in not occurring in the same locus (*ekādhikaraṇāvṛttitva*), because that would exclude antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). Rather, it consists in not occurring at the same time (*ekakālāvṛttitva*).
Thus, the same must be admitted for absolute non-existence as well, as there is no reason for a distinction.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) does not subsist in the time that is the locus qualified by the substratum of the qualifier determined by the objective state (*viṣayatā*) which causes the mention of the negative particle (*nañ*) residing in itself; because it is a non-existence, like prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the others. And absolute non-existence is the state of being a non-existence at all times. The intended goal is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

And thus, when it is established that [the counter-positive] does not subsist at the time that is the locus of the substratum of the counter-correlativity—which consists in such a mode (prakāratā) delimited by such a form—within the subject (pakṣa) delimited by such a form, it follows that the counter-positive, characterized by such a qualified form, is indeed unconnected with time; thereby, the rule is established that all absolute absences (atyantābhāva) have as their counter-positives things that are not grounded in valid cognition (aprāmāṇika).

In order to avoid the occurrence of a *bādha* (contradiction) by taking as the locus of the counter-positive the time residing in the substratum of the qualified form—the absolute absence of cloth—which serves as the locus of the counter-positive and is the substratum of the qualifierhood determined by a subjecthood delimited by the property of being a difference that motivates the mention of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the form "the absolute absence of cloth is not the absolute absence of pot," and likewise to avoid the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example according to that same method, one must instead specify [the counter-positive] as "that which is the objectivity motivating the mention of the word 'is not'."

Furthermore, that [absence] is delimited by a property designated as "relational absence" (*saṃsargābhāvatva*) in the opponent's view—a property distinct from "difference-ness" (*bhedatva*) and such as "prior absence-ness" (*prāgabhāvatva*). Thus, the aforementioned fault does not arise by taking as the object that which is delimited by such "difference-ness. Nor is the reason (*hetu*) inconclusive; for when there is equality in being absences, the assumption—without evidence—that a specific absolute absence has spatial opposition with its aforementioned counter-positive, while other absolute absences (such as those of a rabbit's horn) have temporal opposition, is sublated precisely by the logical difficulty (*tarka*) consisting in prolixity (*gaurava*).

Furthermore, since spatial contradiction necessarily belongs to absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), it would suffice to accept only one kind of occasional absolute non-existence (*sāmayikātyantābhāva*)—namely, that which does not subsist in the locus of its counter-positive at the time of that counter-positive's existence—in order to account for the validity of cognitions such as "the jar does not exist before or after its production. Consequently, the acceptance of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) would be rendered entirely groundless.

Nor can the acceptance of both [prior absence and destruction] be based on the force of the cognitions "a jar will be here" and "a jar has been destroyed here," because the cognition "will be" apprehends that "the jar, as qualified by its occurrence in this place, is related to a time subsequent to this [present]. Furthermore, even properties such as "subsequent-ness" cannot be defined without accepting prior absence and destruction.

Since the indivisible properties of "priority" (*pūrvatva*) and "posteriority" (*uttaratva*), which exist inherently in time and are defined by something else, have been stated by Yādavācārya—the crest-jewel of our school—in his *Tattvasaṃkhyāna-ṭippaṇī* to be non-composite with prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), these two [properties] do not involve such absences. Nor should it be argued that prior absence must be admitted to avoid the consequence of the re-arising of what has already arisen; for "arising" (*utpatti*) is simply the connection of an entity with a moment that was previously unconnected to its preceding moment.

In this regard, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) effects only the connection with a moment; it does not effect even the connection with a preceding moment, because that which already exists by itself cannot be subject to the regulation of a causal complex. Thus, the causal complex of a jar, consisting of a staff and so forth, may bring about the jar’s connection with a moment, but it cannot bring about its "origination" (*utpatti*), which consists in a connection with a specific moment. Therefore, why should one accept the existence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)?

Nor should it be argued that the existence of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is established because its causality is necessary to prevent the re-emergence of a jar—through the force of the causal complex consisting of the stick and other factors—immediately after the destruction of that jar, by means of its connection with a [new] moment.

Even if antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) were accepted, in order to avoid the contingency that a jar—which is to arise only after four moments—would have to exist right now due to the force of the causal complex consisting of the staff and other factors, some unique cause such as that specific moment or action must necessarily be included within the causal complex. Since the aforementioned contingency is thereby averted by the power of that [unique cause] alone, antecedent non-existence is not established. Nor should one abandon antecedent non-existence and likewise destruction (*dhvaṃsa*); rather, let only occasional non-existence (*sāmayikābhāva*) be accepted, having a real entity as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

It should not be argued that the acceptance of unreal counter-correlates (*aprāmāṇika-pratiyogitva*) for the sake of establishing prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest is due to extreme parsimony (*atilāghava*). For the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), it is impossible to say so, as it would entail the fallacy of abandoning one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) and other such consequences. However, this is the answer to the objection raised by a neutral observer: mere parsimony does not determine the actual nature of things. If it did, one might postulate "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and "taste-ness" (*rasatva*) within a single quality, and then have to further postulate that it is grasped by the eye because of its color-ness and by the tongue because of its taste-ness.

Because of parsimony (*lāghava*). Furthermore, there would be only one "blue" and so forth in the entire world, due to parsimony; for when an individual instance perishes or undergoes baking, it could be said that its relation [to the universal] has simply departed. And thus, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the collapse of all established order. Moreover, there would be a contradiction with the sūtra: "And because of desire, there is no dependence on inference.

Therefore, when there is a conflict between perception and scripture, inference and the like do not attain the status of independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of reaching certainty.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Puruṣottamatantro*, when there is mutual contradiction among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), reasoning (*tarka*) characterized by parsimony (*lāghava*) and so forth functions as an auxiliary to one of them in order to establish the object. In the present context, three kinds of non-existence (*abhāva*) are accepted based on their prior, posterior, and eternal natures;
because its nature consists of both existence and non-existence, it is not a separate category of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).

Thus, by means of the words from the *Tattvaviveka* composed by the venerable [Vācaspati Miśra] as cited by the Teacher, together with the words found in the well-known *Śāṇḍilya-tattva* section of the *Vāyu Purāṇa*, and supported by the direct perception that "the jar is destroyed" and "the jar will come to be," it is impossible to deny antecedent negation (*prāgabhāva*), emergent negation (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and absolute negation (*atyantābhāva*)—which are each cognized separately—merely on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*).

By this [argument], the objection of some—who claim that it is useless to postulate that mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) alone is the very nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*), since all arrangements such as "having a counter-correlate" can be maintained by postulating that even absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and the like are the nature of the substratum—is refuted; likewise, the critique of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) found in the *Dīdhiti* and similar works are set aside. This is because we do not accept any entity on the basis of mere reasoning alone, but rather on the authority of statements such as those from the *Tattvaviveka* and the *Vāyu Purāṇa* cited previously, which reveal that difference (*bheda*) alone is the essential nature of things.

However, since the aforementioned objection finds no scope regarding an established fact— by such authoritative evidence cited in the *Taittirīya-bhāṣya* and elsewhere as "But the distinction of all things is their own immutable intrinsic nature"—

there is no harm in our position even for one who disputes those very statements, provided there is no other means of proof. Otherwise, it would follow that even in our own system we must abandon [the authority of the Vedas], because it would be impossible to establish the duty of performing twilight prayers, sacrifices, and so forth by means of the Veda, which would lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for a Buddhist.

Regarding the avoidance of circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) and other such fallacies in the apprehension of difference, the commentators have demonstrated—without insisting that difference is the very nature of the substratum (*dharmi-svarūpa*)—in the *Samayapāda* of the *Anuvyākhyānasudhā* through the presentation of the Naiyāyika view (beginning with "the state of being the substratum, the counter-correlate, and their difference are simultaneous"), as well as in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā* (beginning with "kiñca"). Therefore, there is no utility in insisting upon that [nature of the substratum] during a debate with Advaitins.

And thus, since there is no specific decisive evidence to determine whether the contradiction among the three types of absence—prior absence and the others—is purely temporal with respect to their counter-positive, or whether it is purely spatial in the case of a particular type of absolute absence, there is an occasion for inference aided by principles such as parsimony (*lāghava*).

Moreover, by its very nature, whatever kind of cognition arises from a particular word, it is invariably the case that the conceptualization expressed by that word also possesses that same form. Thus, in the case of "there is no jar on the ground," since what is understood is the absence of a jar possessing existence (sattā) whose locus is the ground, the object of the corresponding verbalized cognition must be stated to be an absence whose counter-positive is such a qualified jar.

On that spot of ground where a jar is well-known, there exists either a prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) or a destruction (dhvaṃsa) whose counter-positive is the qualified entity consisting of that [jar]. Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, prior non-existence and destruction with a "pure" (unqualified) counter-positive would not be established.

In a case where both the jar and its relation have either arisen or perished, one must accept—on the basis of other cognitions such as "the jar and its relation will arise," "it will exist," or "the jar and its relation have perished"—that it is precisely prior non-existences (*prāgabhāva*) and destructions (*dhvaṃsa*) whose qualifiers and qualificands are already established that appear as having a qualified entity as their counter-correlate (*viśiṣṭapratiyogika*). Thus, the fact that [non-existence] has a pure entity as its counter-correlate (*śuddhapratiyogikatva*) is established.

In reality, however, by the very cognition that apprehends color (*rūpa*) in Caitra as qualified by "Caitra-ness" (*caitratva*)—as in "Caitra is colored"—the state of being colored is established even in the pure [substratum]. Otherwise, the pure [substratum] would be colorless. Similarly, by the cognition that apprehends counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) in the qualified, counter-positiveness is indeed made an object even in the pure [substratum].

Alternatively, let it not be that there is an apprehension of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) with respect to that which is qualified by that property (*taddharma*). Let there be an apprehension of it with respect to that which is merely indicated (*upalakṣita*) by that property. Where the counter-positiveness of the absence appearing at that time is sublated in the aspect of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there the counter-positiveness appears either in the qualified [entity] or in the relation between the jar and the ground, which serve as the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). Where a jar does not exist on the ground in any way whatsoever, there the cognition "the jar is not" arises.

In that case, since a jar existing on that ground—which is non-existent [in relation to that absence]—appears as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), it is established that every absolute absence has a non-existent counter-correlate. Nor should it be argued: "Since in cases where the cognition 'the ground is devoid of a jar' arises, the jar appears as the counter-correlate precisely as something unconnected with that very ground, one must therefore admit the existence of absences that have existent counter-correlates."

When the aforementioned cognition is perceptual, then—since the initial cognition "there is no jar on this ground" is necessary—the jar must appear as a non-existent counter-correlative (pratiyogin) there according to the stated method; consequently, because the second cognition, which apprehends the object of that [initial] cognition, must necessarily have an absence with a non-existent counter-correlative as its object, one must resort to the theory of secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) for the word "jar" and so forth occurring in the expressive sentence, [applying it] to a jar or the like residing on the ground.

In a locus where there is an inferential cognition such as "this [locus] possesses the absence of a jar" or a verbal cognition [to that effect], the cognition "there is no jar here" can never be denied by anyone at any time; therefore, it is logically established that even the aforementioned inferential and other cognitions of absence have that [absence] as their object.

Nor should it be argued that from the sentence "There is no jar on the ground," the cognition "the absence of the jar has existence residing in the locus of the ground" or "the absence of the jar residing in the ground has existence as its substrate" is accepted; for since the verbalized cognition (abhilāpyapratīti) also possesses the same object as that [direct] cognition, it apprehends the jar as the counter-correlate (pratiyogin), and thus the status of having a non-existent counter-correlate is not established.

Because the negative particle (*nañ*) has a fixed denotation, it is impossible for the meaning of the verb or other elements to be construed with that which is presented by it; thus, according to the method already stated, such a cognition cannot be expressed. Otherwise, just as the aforementioned sentence would be used in the sense "the absence of a pot residing on the ground is perceptible," there would follow the undesirable consequence of using sentences such as "on the ground, the pot is not perceptible" or "on the ground, the pot is not cognizable."

Furthermore, in cases such as "there are no two pots on the ground" (*bhrātale ghaṭau na staḥ*) or "there are no pots on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭā na santi*), the dual and plural verbal endings would be untenable; for since non-existence is a single entity, duality and so forth cannot be predicated of it. Indeed, in those instances, what is understood is not a pair or a triad of absences. If one were to admit such a thing, it would follow that such cognitions could not arise when there is a single pot or two pots present in the locus.

Nor should it be argued that, even so, one may accept the cognition either as "the absence of existence having the jar as its agent resides on the ground" (*ghaṭakartṛkasattābhāvo bhūtalavṛttiḥ*) or as "the jar, which is the counter-positive of the absence residing on the ground, is the locus of existence. For even by that much, the fact that the counter-positive is something established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) remains unimpaired. This is because, in the first alternative, the locative case following the word *bhūtala* would be untenable; for that [locative] is prescribed only when it signifies the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as determined by the meaning of the verbal root.

Therefore, since it must be stated that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) occurs only with respect to existence (*sattā*), it is established that the object of the cognition is an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is non-empirical; for one must accept that the cognition is precisely of the absence of the existence of a jar, which has the ground as its locus and the jar as its agent. The second alternative, however, is untenable. If that were the case, the sentence "A rabbit's horn does not exist anywhere" would result in being non-authoritative (*aprāmāṇya*), because existence is sublated (*bādhita*) in the case of a rabbit's horn. Furthermore, even in the Nyāya system, the sentence "The sky does not exist on the ground" would result in being non-authoritative.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the expression "there is no fire on the lake or on the mountain" with the intention of conveying the cognition: "fire, which is the counter-positive of the absence residing in the lake, resides on the mountain. Therefore, it is logical that the cognition occurs only in the manner previously stated.

Furthermore, when asked, "Is there a jar on the ground?", one answers, "No. In that case, since it is established that the answer-sentence conveys a meaning connected with the sense of the portion of the question other than the word *kiṃ* (what), and since it is established that such a sentence conveys the cognition of an absence whose counter-positive is qualified by the meaning understood from that sentence, it is necessary that the cognition be of the same nature elsewhere as well. In examples such as "This is not Caitra’s," the absence of the referent of the word *idam* (this) as qualified by the relation to Caitra is what is conveyed by virtue of its non-existence.

Nor should it be argued that what is to be conveyed here is merely the absence of the relation between Caitra and the referent of the word "this" (as expressed by the genitive case), because there is no sublation (bādhaka) here as there is in cases such as "the jar does not exist. And thus, it must be said that an absence whose counter-positive (pratiyogin) is established by valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika) is proven.

Since the sentence "That is not here," which contains the pronoun *tat* (that) as a term signifying the relation to Caitra, conveys an absence whose counter-positive is a real entity other than mere non-existence, one must—due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*)—accept that such a sentence generates a cognition whose object is an absence having a non-existent counter-positive, according to the aforementioned principle. Similarly, this same reasoning should be inferred to apply even when the sentence "Caitra does not cook" is taken to convey an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*).

Indeed, by the arguments stated previously, even from the statement "The jar is not a cloth," there would arise the cognition of the absence of the jar—which is the locus of the becoming performed by the cloth; consequently, since that jar would lack epistemic warrant, the aforementioned sentence would result in conveying only absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), and not the cognition of difference (*bheda*).

And thus, regarding the statement "mutual non-existence is not separate," one might object that this would contradict the commentary by the author of the *Ṭīkā* on the occasion of explaining the root text of the *Tattvaviveka*, where he accepts that the word *bhāva* is derived from a verbal root with the suffix *ghañ* (agentive) and explains: "By the etymology 'that which does not exist mutually,' the word *anyonyābhāva* denotes a possessor of difference (*bhedavān*); then, by the subsequent abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), mutual non-existence itself is denoted. If you raise this objection, we say no.

Since in the expression "a jar is not a cloth," the cloth is construed as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) within the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), namely difference (*bheda*), and that [difference] is construed non-differently (*abhedenānvaya*) with the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) consisting of the act of being (*bhavana*); and since, according to the theory that the meaning of a noun is construed non-differently [with another], in the case of "a jar is not a cloth," the meaning of the figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) negative particle—which is difference—is accepted as being construed non-differently with the referent of the other term, there is no obstacle to the non-differential construal of the meaning of the negative particle (i.e., difference) with the act of being in the present instance.

And thus, the cognition arises that "the jar is the locus of the unique property consisting of the difference from cloth. That the difference from the jar's own nature is uniquely belonging to the jar is beyond dispute.

Alternatively, "becoming" (*bhavana*) is the existence of its own nature (*svarūpasattā*); since this is the nature of the difference from the jar, it resides in the jar, and thus there is no fault. Or else, in the case of "the jar does not become a cloth," the cloth itself is construed as the locus (*āśrayatayā*) in the becoming that consists of the existence of its own nature. Consequently, the resulting cognition is: "the jar is distinct from the locus of the becoming whose agent is the cloth. This occurs under the view that the meaning of the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the agent in the form of a locus, whereby the cognition apprehends a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the meaning of the verb suffix.

Alternatively, within this very view, the cloth has a relation of non-difference with the locus of the meaning of the verb suffix, which is conjoined with the process of becoming (bhavana) that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root. And thus, the cognition arises: "The jar possesses a difference from the agent of the process of becoming whose nature is the cloth."

Alternatively, there is the connection (*anvaya*) of the negation (*nañ*), whose meaning is non-existence, with the existence (*sattā*)—which consists in the coming-into-being of the meaning of the verbal root as qualified by the cloth—with the agent (*kartṛ*), which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) and serves as its substratum (*āśraya*), specifically in relation to the jar. This is because, as in the view of the Guru (Prabhākara) who accepts the cognition "there is an obligation (*kārya*) having the non-existence of eating *kalañja* as its object" in cases such as "one should not eat *kalañja*," it is possible to accept the appearance of the meaning of the negation between the meaning of the verbal root and the meaning of the verbal suffix.

Furthermore, since scholars have accepted that in such statements as "because the other does not arise for one who is not deluded" (*nāmūḍhasyetarotpatteḥ*) and "because [something] does not manifest without having destroyed [its predecessor]" (*nānupamṛdya prādurbhāvāt*), an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the base of the ablative case (*pañcamīprakṛti*) is construed with the meaning of the ablative; therefore, in this interpretation, the absence of existence in the agent of the cloth is simply the nature of its difference from it. Thus, in all these positions, the capacity to convey difference is successfully established.

Now, why is this [interpretation] accepted? One might ask: "Why not assume that the negation of the jar is like the existence of the cloth's agent, as in 'there is no jar on the ground' and so forth? This is not so. For in that case, if one were to understand the absence of the jar's agent-existence on the ground, the locative case in "on the ground" (*bhūtale*) would be untenable; and just as the aforementioned untenability applies when the meaning of the verb is construed with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), there is no such untenability regarding the first [case-ending] and so forth when the understanding is accepted according to the stated method. Furthermore, when asked, "What, does the jar become a cloth?", one says "No."

In that case, according to the method previously stated by you, it is necessary for you that the sentence [‘The jar is not a cloth’] conveys the negation of a jar qualified by the state of being a cloth-maker. Likewise, because it is established—on the basis of the expression ‘There is no identity of cloth in the jar’—that such a cognition has as its object the absence of the identity of cloth residing in the jar, it follows accordingly that the cognition ‘The jar is not a cloth’ also [has as its object the absence of identity], just as in the case of ‘This is not Caitra’s,’ according to the method already mentioned.

It must be stated that this [cognition] has as its object precisely the absence of identity between the pot and the cloth; how, then, can there be any hope for it to have difference (*bheda*) as its object? To this it must be replied: since the cognition expressed by the verbal statement "The pot is distinct from the cloth"—which is established by experience as having negation as its object—must necessarily have as its object a difference that is distinct from absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), so too the fact that even a cognition of the mere form "This is indeed a pot" has as its object a unique entity in the form of self-nature difference (*svarūpabheda*) is difficult to deny.

Even in the case of "The pot is not a cloth," it is established by experience that the cognition of "it does not exist" and so forth has as its object a locus (anuyogin) qualified by a nature such as "difference" (bhedatva), which is distinct from the mere [negative] locus appearing in such cognitions. Nor should it be argued that because the verb "exists" (bhavati) is supplied in the verbal expression, what appears there is the very non-existent pot—qualified by its existence as a cloth—as the counter-positive (pratiyogin) of a negation in the form of absolute non-existence; for this would contradict universal experience.
This is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (non-presuppositional negation) where the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with a verb;
it should be understood as a *paryudāsa* (presuppositional exclusion) where the negative particle is connected with the following word.

Thus, by this verse, the learned have stated that in cases such as "the jar is not a cloth" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo na*), the negative particle (*nañ*) is designated as *paryudāsa* (exclusion) because it conveys a distinction (*bheda*) whose own meaning is related to the meaning of the subsequent word, namely the word "cloth. Since it is stated here that comprehension occurs even without the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of a verb, whereas it is stated that a verb is necessary in instances where there is the cognition of a relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*) consisting of *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), it follows that in the latter case, the ellipsis of an unexpressed verb is indispensable.

In expressions such as "the ground is without a jar" (*aghaṭaṃ bhūtalam*) or "free from flies" (*nirmakṣikam*), the capacity to convey absolute non-existence even without an expressed action is established solely by the force of the grammatical rules prescribing such compounds. In those cases, the manifestation of a non-existence whose counter-positive is non-existent is to be understood through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) according to the method previously stated. Furthermore, since identity (*abheda*) is already established by the aforementioned cognitions, there is no complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating that the sentence "the jar becomes a cloth" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo bhavati*) and the cognition expressed by it have that [identity] as their object.

The commentary on the *Tattvaviveka* is indeed appropriate; for, since the cognition produced by the sentence "A pot is not a cloth" possesses the same object as the effect of that cognition—namely, the linguistic usage "A pot is distinct from a cloth"—which occurs without any intervening knowledge, it follows without impediment that, by virtue of being the generator of such usage, the cognition produced by the sentence "A pot is not a cloth" unassailably conveys mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), according to the method described above.

Granted that, in some cases, the sentence "Does a pot become a cloth?"—through its association with the word *nañ* (negation)—may convey the negation of a pot characterized by the becoming of a cloth; yet, this much does not, by the reasoning stated immediately above, deprive the aforementioned sentence of its status as having mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) as its object. From the statement "There is no identity of cloth in the pot," there arises the cognition of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the unreal identity of cloth residing in the pot.

The practical effect, such as the linguistic usage "the jar is distinct from the cloth," is accepted as occurring precisely through the arising of either an inference based on the difference of their respective marks (*talliṅgakabhedānumiti*) or a mental cognition (*mānasajñāna*); for such [cognitions] do not arise in those who lack the apprehension that the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*) is pervaded by difference. Thus, everything is faultless.

However, some maintain that since the Naiyāyikas accept that the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of a thing is essentially the difference from that which possesses it, and since there is no evidence for a difference between the two entities under discussion, the matter ultimately resolves to that very point; furthermore, because an absolute absence that is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*) is not accepted in the final system (*siddhānta*), such an absolute absence is indeed a difference.

As for the pure absolute absence (*śuddhātyantābhāva*), however, it is universally present (*kevalānvayin*) and has only unestablished (*aprāmāṇika*) counter-correlates; thus, there is no contradiction with the rule that a pure absolute absence necessarily has an unestablished counter-correlative.

The purity of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) consists in its possessing that nature of absolute non-existence which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) of each and every such counter-correlation that defines the absolute non-existence residing in the difference (*bheda*) that constitutes the very essence of whatever substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is qualified by the nature of the absolute non-existence of whichever respective counter-correlate.

Whatever the counter-positiveness residing in the jar belonging to the absolute absence of a jar may be, the substrata characterized by that absolute absence which has that [counter-positiveness] as its determiner are the various substrata distinct from those possessing jars; and the absences consisting of those [substrata] are the absences of what possesses a jar, being identical with their own respective natures. This is because it has been established that the nature of difference belongs to an absolute absence whose counter-positive is a real entity, and the nature of the absolute absence of a jar resides in those [absences].

Whichever counter-correlatives (*pratiyogitā*) are defined by that [absence] reside only in real entities such as jars and the like. Any other [counter-correlative], such as a rabbit’s horn, resides in the non-existent (*asat*), because it is impossible to employ such a term as "of such-and-such a kind" (*yādṛśa*) with respect to it. To explain: if the counter-correlativity residing in a rabbit’s horn were of such a nature, then whatever substrata (*adhikaraṇa*)—such as the ground—are qualified by being the locus of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) defined by that [counter-correlativity], the various differences (*bheda*) consisting of those very substrata would be differences whose counter-correlates are distinct categories of entities.

That which is the nature of absolute non-existence residing therein—namely, the nature of the non-existence of a rabbit’s horn—is not of the nature of a difference (bheda) identical with that [locus], because it lacks the status of being the very essence of the substratum (dharmin). Rather, according to the aforementioned method, it is simply the nature of the absolute non-existence of a jar. The status of being its determiner does not belong to the counter-positiveness (pratiyogitā) residing in things such as a rabbit’s horn. In this context, if one disregards the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) "whatever is a locus," then even the counter-positiveness residing in a rabbit’s horn would indeed be of that same nature.

Since the absence of a rabbit’s horn exists even in itself, the locus characterized by the state of being an absolute absence whose counter-positive resides in the rabbit’s horn is indeed the absence of the rabbit’s horn. The difference consisting of that [absence] is the difference from a pot residing in it. The state of being an absolute absence residing in that [difference] is the state of being the absolute absence of a rabbit’s horn, because it is the determiner (nirūpaka) of that [absence]. Therefore, this [latter] is what is intended.

It should be understood that the phrase "the locus of an absence having such-and-such a counter-positive" (*yādṛśapratiyogitākābhāvādhikaraṇa*) is sufficient for completion; the addition of the term "substratum of absolute non-existence" (*atyantābhāvatvāśraya*) is intended to indicate that the counter-positiveness of an absolute non-existence other than that [in question] is to be grasped by the word *yādṛśa* (such-and-such), and not for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Alternatively, "purity" (*śuddhatva*) may simply consist in being different from a negative inference (*vyatirekin*). Since absolute non-existences whose counter-positives are established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*)—which consist of the difference from the very nature of various substrates—are themselves negative inferences, that [over-extension] is thereby excluded.

By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "If purity consists in being other than difference, then even the non-existence of a hare's horn and the like would be included [among pure things], because they possess the nature of difference residing in themselves; for, by virtue of having themselves as their locus, they consist in a difference whose nature is that of their own locus. This is rejected because there is no fault in either of the two definitions provided above.

Nor does it follow that if the absolute absence of potness (*ghaṭatvātyantābhāva*) were identical in nature with the difference consisting of the cloth (*paṭātmakabheda*), there would be a contradiction with the *Sudhā*, the *Tattvasaṃkhyāna-Ṭīkā*, and other texts which refute the view that an absolute absence is identical with its locus; for in those contexts, the discussion is conducted specifically in terms of "absence" (*abhāvatva*), and thus refers to pure absolute absence, as well as to the pot, its relation, destruction, prior non-existence, and so forth.

But surely, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because for absolute non-existences such as those whose counter-positiveness is delimited by a relation residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa-sambandha*), a difference delimited by that same relation is unestablished; thus, those which are not of that nature—namely, the purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) absolute non-existences possessing a real counter-positive—lack the status of having a non-existent counter-positive. Nor can it be argued that the difference from that [counter-positive] in respect of that relation is itself of the nature of its absolute non-existence and is purely positive, and therefore it does not possess the aforementioned "purity" (*śuddhatva*).

If it is argued that, although one accepts a difference whose counter-correlate is the non-existence of "that-like" [form] by the force of common cognition, one does not cognize "that which possesses it is not," and therefore one does not accept a difference from non-existence in the case of a specific instance of non-existence—this is not so. For since the nature of relation, such as being the delimiting factor of counter-correlation, will be refuted later, we shall instead accept that [the relation] has as its counter-correlate form qualified by being the counter-correlate of conjunction; thus, because that [non-existence] is indeed non-existent, there is no deviation [in the rule].

Furthermore, it cannot be argued that the absence whose counter-positive is established by the valid cognition "there is a bird here" in the case of space—given the non-acceptance of all-pervasive absences—is not to be described as having the nature of a difference consisting of a specific part, existing through a spatial restriction (aṃśavyavasthā), because there is no absence of difference having another part as its counter-positive within that very part; therefore, since it must be an entirely distinct entity, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the attainment of purity. This is what must be stated.

They say: "In that case, the very same counter-positiveness (pratiyogitā) residing in the bird-conjunction existing in one part, which is the definitor of the absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) whose nature is the difference consisting of a jar, is also the definitor of the non-existence that is not a difference residing in another part; thus, because there is an absence of being a definitor of a counter-positiveness other than those [specific ones], and because it is a negative concomitant (vyatirekin) by virtue of not occurring in the part that is the locus of the counter-positive, the state of being 'pure' (śuddhatva) does not exist therein. Furthermore, since it is accepted that the non-existence present there consists of specificities (viśeṣa) standing in the place of the difference between parts, or because both the difference and the specificity must be included in the definition, there is no fault."

Now, it might be argued that since all absolute non-existences (*atyantābhāva*) are purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) and thus co-extensive (*samaniyata*), they would necessarily become one and the same. Consequently, attributes such as "faultlessness" could not serve as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Lord, as they would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to living beings (*jīva*) and others. Furthermore, the statement "there is no jar on the ground" would remain valid even when a jar is present on that ground, while the statement "the absence of a jar does not exist on a ground occupied by a jar" would fail to be a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Moreover, the reasoning that existence and non-existence consist in mutual exclusion (*parasparavirahātmakatva*) would also be untenable. To this, we reply: no.

Even if there is co-extensiveness (*samaniyatatva*), it is impossible for identity to be established by mere parsimony (*lāghava*) alone without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that proves such identity. Otherwise, there would be identity even among "nameability" (*abhidheyatva*), "knowability" (*jñeyatva*), and so forth, as well as the fifty phonemes, the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), space (*ākāśa*), and the like, all of which are co-extensive in terms of place and time. If you argue that this is not the case for those [latter] because they are positive entities (*bhāvatva*), then let there likewise be a difference between these [phonemes] precisely because they are negative entities (*abhāvatva*).

If you argue that this is not so because there is a perception of difference—such as "the letter *ka* was heard by me, not the letter *ga*"—since these [letters] are experienced as having properties distinct from those such as being an action (*kriyā*) and so forth, then consider this: after hearing the sentence "A rabbit's horn does not exist," and after waiting for some time, one who has heard "A man's horn does not exist" would perceive in such a manner: "Previously the absence of a rabbit's horn was heard, not the absence of a man's horn; now this [absence] is heard, not that. And so forth.

Since difference is perceived, and because there is the experience of distinctness in the various factors such as doubt—which are the effects of those respective cognitions—and since non-existences (abhāva) possess unique properties consisting in their being related to their own respective counter-correlates (pratiyogin), let there also be a difference among these non-existences.

Nor is there any inconsistency in "faultlessness" being a definition of the Lord (Bhagavat), for it is accepted that the definition of the Lord is the state of possessing the absence of faults residing in Himself. For this very reason, it was refined in the *Mandāramañjarī* thus: "Beginninglessness is the state of not being the counter-correlative of one's own prior non-existence."

If it is argued: "But surely, since the word 'own' (sva) refers to that which is mentioned in proximity, even if the Lord is understood by the word 'own' in a definition-statement of the Lord, the definition would still result in the very absence of the fault of being resident in the Lord; thus, its over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the individual soul (*jīva*) remains unavoidable," we say no. For otherwise, the definition stated in the *Mandāramañjarī* would likewise have to be rejected.

Even there, although [the term] "beginningless" is expressed by its own word, it follows that the definition would result in being either (1) the absence of being the counter-positive of a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) whose counter-positive is beginningless, or (2) the absence of that which is the state of being the counter-positive of a prior non-existence residing in what is beginningless; and because this is obtained as the definition, its over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to things that have a beginning (*sādi*) is unavoidable.

If it is argued that what is intended by that sentence as the definition is the qualified entity (viśiṣṭa) which is the object of the valid cognition produced by the sentence "This is that which lacks the counter-positiveness of its own prior non-existence," then here too there is no stated defect; for we accept that the definition is the very same qualified entity which is the object of the valid cognition produced by the sentence "This [person] is one who lacks defects residing in himself," taken in its identity (tādātmya).

Nor should it be argued that, since the sentence "and not like the absence of defects" can also convey the absence of both [defects and excellence], the individual soul (jīva) would also be a qualified object of such valid cognition; for valid cognition must be qualified by being opposed to a cognition whose qualifier is delimited by the property of "defect-ness," whereas a cognition of the absence of both is not so opposed.

There is no fault here; for there is no defect if the definition intends to refer to that qualified entity which is the object of the valid cognition expressed by the sentence "this [person] is devoid of defects," a cognition that arises in the moment immediately following the valid cognition [of the absence of defects]. The definition characterized by beginninglessness (*anāditva*) should also be refined in this very manner; otherwise, it would be incoherent if one were to take as the basis the valid cognition of the absence of both [defects and beginninglessness] as previously stated.

However, some maintain that "faultlessness" (nirdoṣatva) is intended to mean simply the possession of a mode delimited by the relation of locus-ness, which is itself determined by a mode delimited by the relation of counter-correlativity, which in turn is determined by a qualificand-ness residing in the absence of faults as established by valid cognition (*pramā*). Thus, the definition applies to God (*īśvara*) by taking into account such a mode as is established by the valid cognition: "There are no faults in God."

For even though that which appears as possessing a connection with a defect appearing as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) does not exist in the form of such a composite (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), it must nevertheless be established that the pure [object] also appears subsequently; thus, the appearance of that [pure object] is admitted. If that were not accepted, however, let the definition simply be "being the locus of the objective state (*viṣayatā*) that sustains such a mode (*prakāratā*)," because otherwise, prior to the presentation of God (*īśvara*), such a mode could not be sustained as appearing as connected with its counter-correlate in a subsequent cognition regarding what is non-existent.

This is because, by the force of common understanding alone, one accepts that the subjecthood (viṣayatā) residing in Īśvara, which was previously present, is the cause of such a mode (prakāratā). Furthermore, since the cognition "there is no defect in the individual soul" lacks the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), the definition [of falsity] applies there according to the aforementioned method. Likewise, regarding the beginninglessness of the definition itself, the refinement follows the same method if its meaning is taken to be the absence of that state of being the counter-positive of its own prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) which resides in itself.

However, if the meaning is formulated in the manner beginning with "one's own prior non-existence" (*svasya yaḥ prāgabhāvaḥ*), then it should be refined according to the following principle: "the state of being a locus of the objective condition (*viṣayatā*) that motivates the objective condition of the prior non-existence, which is itself the objective condition of the prior non-existence, as determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) delimited by the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-saṃsarga*) as determined by the objective condition of such a non-existence."

As for the objection—how can there be a status as a qualifier (*prakāratā*) belonging to prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) when everything appearing within the scope of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is non-existent—it is to be refuted by the direction that will be explained later: that such a status consists simply in being the cause for the employment of words such as "that" (*tat-śabda*). They say that this should be understood similarly in other cases as well.

Likewise, the sentence "there is no jar here" does not possess validity with respect to a ground that actually contains a jar. This is because that sentence establishes the cognition of an absolute absence whose counter-positive is a jar conjoined with that very ground; thus, the property of having as its counter-positive a jar conjoined with the locus of the jar—which must be conveyed by that sentence regarding the absolute absence—is sublated. Nor is it reasonable to attribute validity to the sentence "this [ground] possesses the absence of a jar."

This is because you yourself have accepted the validity of such sentences as having the intention of conveying the non-existence of both [the jar and its absence], and this is likewise desired by me; for it has already been stated that in cases where the intention is to convey a general absence, words such as "jar" are used figuratively (lākṣaṇika) to denote the jar and so forth as being connected with the co-occurring locus, and thus, according to the aforementioned reasoning, such a sentence would possess a sublated meaning.

The argument that the authority of statements such as "free from desire" (*niraniṣṭa*) and "free from fault" (*niravadya*) might pertain to the individual soul (*jīva*) is also refuted by this very [point]. For if those sentences were to have the individual soul as their object, it would necessarily follow—by the force of logic—that they convey the absence of defects residing in the soul; however, such a state of affairs is contradicted [by experience].

Nor should it be argued that the sentence "the individual soul possesses that absence which is understood from the statement 'He is without end, etc. would lack validity; for the absence whose counter-positive is a defect residing in God exists in the individual soul as well. This is because such an absence is accepted by those who maintain its status as a *kevalānvayin* (an absolute universal). Otherwise, the very mention of its being a *kevalānvayin* would result in inconsistency. Likewise, even the sentence "there is no absence of a jar on the ground where there is a jar" is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Since the word "pot" (ghaṭa) has been established as referring to a pot conjoined with that particular ground—based on the unauthoritative statement "there is no pot here"—the sentence "there is no absence of the pot here" also produces the cognition: "the absolute absence of that absence which is the counter-positive of the pot conjoined with this ground. And that [cognition] is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*).

On that ground where a jar exists, there is an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is a jar conjoined with that ground; since such a jar is utterly non-existent, the absolute absence of it—which is the object of that cognition—necessarily exists. Consequently, a sentence such as "It is not here," which contains a pronoun (*tatpada*) denoting an exclusively positive entity (*kevalānvayi*) in the form of an absolute absence whose counter-positive is a jar conjoined with some other ground, is simply invalid (*apramāṇa*). This is because the specific individuality (*vyakti*) of that absence, qualified by its subsistence in this particular ground, exists, and thus the absolute absence [of that absence] is sublated (*bādhita*).

Thus, the statement that existence and non-existence consist in their mutual exclusion is also according to the perspective of other schools. In our own system, however, following the cognition "there is no jar here," there arises a true knowledge (*yathārthajñāna*) to the effect that "this place possesses the absence of a jar"; the state of being pervaded by that which constitutes the qualified object (*viśiṣṭa*) of such knowledge is the nature of the jar's absence as being the exclusion of the jar. Similarly, by the method of "there is no absence of a jar here" and so forth, the nature of the jar is its being the exclusion of the absence of a jar.

And pervadedness (*vyāpyatā*) is to be understood as being the object of a subsequent cognition that is produced by the very cognition in which the negative particle (*nañ*) is mentioned. Therefore, there is no loss of its pervadedness even if it is a purely positive universal (*kevalānvayin*). In this manner, that [pervadedness] is merely technical (*pāribhāṣika*). Alternatively, for an absence, pervadedness consists in having as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) the object of a superimposition (*āropa*) where that [absence] itself is the primary factor; or, it results in the state of being the locus of the objectivity (*viṣayatā*) belonging to a valid cognition (*pramā*), which is determined by a qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) delimited by a relation of counter-positive-ness, and which is brought about by the objectivity residing in itself [the absence].

In the case of a positive entity (*bhāva*), however, it is defined technically (*pāribhāṣika*) as "being the locus of that objective content which serves as the cause for the objective content of the counter-positive. In cases such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), because the counter-positive actually exists, the objective content of the counter-positive itself is the cause for the objective content of the counter-positive as apprehended by the cognition of non-existence. In the case of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), however, according to the view stated by some, it is the objective content of the primary object—which is actually existent—that serves as the cause.

In this regard, if the objective reference delimited by the general property *ghaṭatva* (potness) is the determinant, then the absence whose primary element is the general is designated by the term "general absence" (*sāmānyābhāva*). However, when the primary element is delimited by a specific property, it becomes a "specific absence" (*viśeṣābhāva*); thus, the distinction between them is established. The absence established by the cognition "there is no horn on a rabbit" has the horn as its primary element. The absence established by the cognition "there is no rabbit-horn anywhere" likewise has the rabbit-horn as its primary element alone.

Even for that which is non-existent (*asat*), it is logical that it possesses "primacy" (*pradhānatva*)—as intended in the present context—in the sense of being the locus of such a cognitive objecthood (*viṣayatā*). Since existence and non-existence consist in the aforementioned absence [of the other], their mention is indeed purposeful, as it is somehow useful for the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of sentences that convey existence and non-existence. Other points may likewise be inferred; enough of this elaboration.

The teachers residing at Vaṃśapallī, however, having refined the definition of "faultlessness" as "the state of not being the object of a cognition preceded by the superimposition of a fault," and having accepted that even an absence whose counter-positive is non-existent stands in contradiction with whatever is primary in that superimposition, they avoided the over-extension [of the definition] to the individual soul (jīva).

In their view, although all absolute absences (*atyantābhāva*) are alike in having non-existent things as their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), there is a systematic distinction regarding the invalidity of statements such as "there is no jar on the ground where a jar exists" or "this [ground] possesses the absence of a jar. Consequently, an absence whose primary correlate is existent is a negative-only (*vyatirekin*) probans, being primarily opposed to what is existent; whereas one whose primary correlate is non-existent is a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) probans. Furthermore, the refinement of the mutual exclusion between existence and non-existence as stated in the *Taraṅgiṇī* is also to be resolved according to this school's perspective.

Thus, regarding the rule that absence must have a real (prāmāṇika) counter-positive, they say that other minor objections of this kind should be avoided by those of subtle intellect; enough has been said on this matter.

However, Satyanātha Śrīcaraṇa, in works such as the *Abhinavatāṇḍava*, establishes even absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) as having a real counter-positive within his system, thereby abandoning that restrictive rule. In his view, every systematic arrangement becomes easily established. The method of this establishment should be sought in his own work itself; for fear of making the present treatise too voluminous, it is not elaborated here.

If it is argued that this dispute regarding experience is therefore endless, we reply: no, because it is also sublated by reasoning (*yukti*). To explain: if one does not accept that [the cognition of] "being apprehended as the absence of the probandum" (*sādhyābhāvatvena avagāhitva*) is the cause [of inferential error], then one must instead maintain that the cause is the cognition of being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the actual absence of the probandum (*tadvyāpakābhāvapratiyogitvajñāna*). If that were the case, then since the absence of color (*rūpābhāva*) is itself of the nature of the non-absence of that color, there would arise the erroneous inference of the absence of color in a jar, due to the cognition that the jar possesses "jar-ness," which is the counter-positive of the absence that pervades that color.

Likewise, in the case where the probandum is a positive entity (*bhāva-sādhya*), there would arise the undesirable consequence of an inference—such as "there is fire on the mountain"—having a non-present probandum as its primary qualificand. This would occur because a cognition of smoke possessing a counter-positive that is the absence pervading that specific instance [of fire] would apprehend the absence of fire through its specific individuality (*tadvyaktitvena*). To avoid this, one might accept such an inference in cases where the probandum is an absence (*abhāva-sādhya*) but refuse it in cases where the probandum is a positive entity; however, this would result in the fallacy of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) argument, which applies inconsistent criteria to similar cases.

Nor should it be argued that the "individuality residing in an absence" (tadvyaktitva) whose counter-correlate is an entity is difficult to define as something distinct from its being the counter-correlate of a specific counter-positive; for, just as in the case of color and so forth, the individuality residing in that [absence] exists there precisely without being constituted by the counter-positive. Otherwise, at the time of cosmic dissolution when all fire is destroyed, the individuality residing in that absence would also be subject to destruction; consequently, lacking the nature of that individuality, it would either be identical with other things or be devoid of its own nature (niḥsvarūpa).

Furthermore, when Caitra says, "Whatever exists on the mountain," an inference would unavoidably arise from the following *parāmarśa* (reflective cognition): "The counter-positive of an absence that pervades [the mountain], which is the object intended by that particular word 'whatever' uttered by Caitra at that time"—a cognition which apprehends the absence of fire as being the object intended by that particular word. Thus, from a *parāmarśa* regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) defined by the absence of denotability, an erroneous inference of the absence of denotability would be produced from a fallacious negative inference (*vyatirekyābhāsa*). That [erroneous inference] ought not to occur.
In that case, since the probandum itself is unestablished, its real absence is likewise non-existent; therefore, the delimiting condition for causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) is absent therein.

Nor should it be argued that even if one accepts another cause consisting of the real absence of the probandum, the status of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the form of a negation as the cause is not abandoned, and thus an inference from a fallacious negative mark (*vyatirekyābhāsa-liṅga*) is possible solely through a reflective awareness that is essentially an error possessing a subject-object relation (*viṣayitā*) characterized by the relationship of the determined and the determiner (*nirūpyanirūpakabhāva*).

This is because, in your view—which accepts the aforementioned alternative cause—it would be impossible to avoid the consequence that the inference "there is an absence of denotability in the cloth" (derived from the cognition "the cloth possesses the absence of potness, which is the counter-positive of the absence that pervades denotability") would be a fallacious negative inference (*vyatirekyābhāsa*). This is since, just as the cognition "the lake possesses the absence of fire, which is the counter-positive of the absence that pervades smoke" leads to the inference of the absence of smoke in the lake, so too would the cognition "the cloth possesses the absence of potness, which is the counter-positive of the absence that pervades denotability" lead to the inference of the absence of denotability in the cloth; and yet, in the case of that [latter] parāmarśa, the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of the cause you have stated is absent. This is the intended meaning.

By this, the claim that "the cause is a cognition which apprehends pervasion as qualified by the counter-correlativity of the absence that has become the probandum" is refuted; for in the aforementioned instance, the very absence that constitutes the probandum is unestablished.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that, in an inference where the probandumness is delimited by absenceness as determined by a subject-ness delimited by a particular property (D), the cause of the *parāmarśa*—namely, the ascertainment of an absence whose counter-positivehood is delimited by a property grasped as the delimitor of pervasion with respect to that [property D]—is accepted as being a cause common to both such cognitions; for this very reason, the author of the *Dīdhiti* stated exactly so in the section on negative inference (*vyatirekin*). And thus, no previously mentioned defect arises.

"Mountain possesses the absence of smoke, because it possesses the absence of that which is delimited by a property that delimits the pervasion of what is delimited by the property of being smoke. Alternatively, this may be established through the knowledge of a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*): "Whatever possesses the absence of a counter-positive delimited by a property that delimits the pervasion of what is delimited by a certain property, that [locus] possesses the absence of that [property]. If one objects to the lack of a commonality (*ananugama*) regarding the variables *yat* and *tat*, then one may employ specific pervasions: "Whatever possesses the aggregate (*kūṭa*) of absences of specific instances of a certain thing, that possesses the absence of that thing in general"; or "Whatever is a particular reason (*hetu*), that is pervaded by its [corresponding] universal"; or "Whatever is an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*)..."

Regarding the means for accomplishing that [completion], such as in the rule "he who is whose son shall take his wealth," although properties such as being *yat* (that), *tat* (this), the state of being a reason (*hetutva*), the state of being a probandum (*sādhyatva*), auspiciousness (*maṅgalatva*), and completion (*samāptitva*) lack any commonality (*anugatatva*), one accepts an inference there by means of a cognition that apprehends another form of pervasion—which takes the place of a general pervasion—in order to account for the inference established by experience. Since it is possible to accept an inference in the present case in exactly the same way, we do not admit that the aforementioned negative consideration (*vyatireki-parāmarśa*) is what actually brings about the result.

Nor would it be the case that [the inference] does not have the absence delimited by fire-ness (*vahnitva*) as its logical mark (*liṅga*); rather, it must indeed have as its logical mark the absence delimited by fire-ness which is the delimitor of the pervasion of smoke. This is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because an inferential cognition having as its logical mark the absence delimited by fire-ness arises precisely at a stage when there is no manifestation of that [specific] form [of the absence].

It must be stated that for that very reason, the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is also accepted as a factor [in inference]. For the *parāmarśa* you favor—namely, "that which possesses the absence of fire, which is the pervader of smoke"—is itself of the nature of the manifestation of the probans (*liṅga*) established by me; thus, its non-manifestation is simply unestablished. However, immediately following that, you accept an inference in the form "there is an absence of smoke on the mountain," which contradicts experience, and from that, you further accept another inference: "it possesses the absence of smoke."

At the time when the probandum (*sādhya*) is already established, many unauthentic assumptions are made—such as that the establishment of the probandum acts as an inhibitor to an inference where the probandum is the qualificand (*viśeṣyaka*), in order to prevent such an inference. I, however, accept only an inference where the probandum is the qualifier (*prakāraka*), as established by universal experience, through the manifestation of general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) and so forth after a delay of two moments. This is because the production of inference during the infinitesimal moment (*sūkṣmakāla*) you favor can only be determined by an oath.

In this regard, our own position alone is logical. For, in a case where there is knowledge of another mark (*liṅga*) qualified by positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*)—as favored by us—at a different time, the inference can be accounted for simply by the force of the two-fold causal complex already established in accordance with that inference, even if one accepts a delay of two moments or more. It is unnecessary to postulate an additional causal complex to account for an inference whose object (*sādhya*) is merely imagined (and thus lacks empirical warrant), nor is it necessary to postulate a counter-argument against the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyaprasiddhi*), because such a course would involve excessive complexity (*atigaurava*) and must therefore be rejected.

And thus, even in the case of the two cognitions "Fire is the pervader of smoke" and "This [locus] possesses the absence of fire," the inference must be accounted for by accepting the cognition of the reason—namely, the absence of fire which is the pervader of smoke—which arises from those [two cognitions]. Otherwise, even in the case of a positive concomitance (*anvayin*), one would have to refrain from postulating a qualified reflective awareness (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*) following the two cognitions.

Precisely because of the aforementioned parsimony (*lāghava*), since the inference of identity with a tree (*vṛkṣatādātmya*) and so forth is possible, the ancients—who do not accept that a tree is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) by way of identity—do not admit pervasion through a relation that does not restrict its occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka-sambandha*). Therefore, it is rightly stated that "because a cognition in the form of a negation cannot be precluded," it is logically sound that only the negative consideration (*vyatireki-parāmarśa*), which apprehends the absence of the probandum as being the absence of the probandum, is the cause of inference.

Alternatively, having accepted what has been stated by others regarding a different type of negative inference (*vyatirekin*), this sentence is intended to demonstrate the impossibility of that method within the very scope of the inference under discussion. In that case, the phrase beginning with "abhāva" (non-existence) serves to include the fact that the cause of inferential reflection (*parāmarśa*) must not involve a cognition of the form of a negation, which is what [the opponent] seeks to establish.

The meaning is as follows: likewise, in a case where non-existence is the probandum (*sādhya*), although an inference such as "there is a difference from water in the jar" might arise from a subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*)—namely, "the jar possesses odor, which is the counter-positive of an absence pervading water by way of identity, while [the jar] is apprehended as water"—nevertheless, in the present inference, it is impossible to avoid the necessity of a subsumptive reflection that apprehends the absence of the probandum as being the absence of the probandum in the form of "being different from all six [categories]."

If it is asked why, it is because "being distinct from both existence and non-existence" means being distinct from non-existence as qualified by its distinction from existence. However, the absence of such a qualified probandum (*sādhya*) does not consist of existence and non-existence. This is because the absence of a qualified entity is perceived as one and the same in both existence and non-existence; since existence and non-existence are mutually non-co-located (*parasparāsamānādhikaraṇa*), their identity is impossible.

If it is argued that the cognition of the unity of non-existence itself depends upon the unity of the nature of non-existence—just as there is a cognition of the unity of the absence of color residing in a jar and a cloth, even though colors are essentially the absence of the absence of color—the answer is no. For even if that were so, by accepting such a cognition according to the reasoning beginning with "being the pervader of the absence of being different from both existent and non-existent," the very form of negation (pratiṣedhākāratva) would necessarily result.

If one accepts an inference based on a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) in the form: "It possesses sublatedness, which is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the existent" (*sad-vyāpakībhūtābhāva-pratiyogi-bādhyatvavān*), and likewise, "It possesses sublatedness, which is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the non-existent" (*asad-vyāpakībhūtābhāva-pratiyogi-bādhyatvavān*), then the resulting inference would also necessarily be of the nature of a collective cognition. It would not have as its predicate (*vidheya*) the probandum (*sādhya*) consisting of being distinct from the existent qualified by being distinct from the non-existent. For in that case, since the distinction from the non-existent is already established in the shell-silver (*śukti-rūpya*), it would be impossible to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhanatā*) with respect to that part.

It was for this very reason that the perception "this is indeed false silver" was previously cited as apprehending a nature distinct from both [existence and non-existence], which is admitted by both parties. Nor should it be argued that if sublation occurs by way of the principle "two in one," then the inferential cognition (parāmarśa) apprehending those two types of counter-correlativity would result in an inference apprehending both existence-distinctness and non-existence-distinctness by way of the principle "two in one. This is because there is no "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*), since such a cognition of that specific form was not previously established; for such cognitions are not supported by valid means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇika*).

Alternatively, even if [the cognition] were valid, there is no evidence for a causal relation between the inferential cognition and the subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) in such a form; thus, because there is an absence of the apprehension of the additional element within the scope of the delimitor of the property to be proved (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*), there is indeed the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) with respect to that part. This has also been stated: because a cognition in the form of a negation—namely, the cognition of the shell as being distinct from reality (*sad-vilakṣaṇatva*) regarding silver—is not prevented, the meaning is that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established with respect to that part.

If, from a logical reflection (*parāmarśa*) such as "being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades both existence and non-existence," there were to arise an inferential cognition (*anumiti*) apprehending a difference qualified by "bothness" (*ubhayatva*), then—since the dual nature of the shell-silver (*śukti-rajata*) is not admitted—it would clearly result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

Even if you argue that by carefully examining the definition of "either-or" (*anyatara*) as "that which pervades either existence or non-existence," the desired conclusion is established because inference also apprehends the absence of being delimited by either-ness, this is still untenable.
