For "either-ness" consists in possessing an absence whose counter-correlate is delimited by the absence of non-existence qualified by the absence of existence; however, since the delimitors of such a counter-correlate—namely, the aforementioned absence of existence qualified by the absence of non-existence—are unestablished (*aprasiddha*), it is impossible for you to prevent the cognition that "the apprehension of pervasion [based on] that [definition] is not possible," which takes the form of a negation regarding the apprehension of pervasion.

Now, it is said that "either-or-ness" (*anyataratva*) is simply the absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the difference from that, the difference from this, and the state of being both; and the apprehension of that [absence] is possible even through the apprehension of each respective difference.

Even then, since such a pair [of existence and non-existence] does not exist, the cognition in the form of a negation—which is rooted in the apprehension of their contradiction—cannot prevent people from engaging with the aforementioned inference even in cases such as "silver in mother-of-pearl," just as it cannot in cases like "the horn of a hare" or "a pot. Consequently, the absence of the reason (hetu), which consists in being sublated, cannot prevent the cognition that negates its pervasion. By this, it is established that the object of the inferential cognition is a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a delimiting factor (avacchedakatā) that is itself delimited by an intrinsic relation (svarūpa-sambandha) residing in the state of being existent, non-existent, or both.

Therefore, there is no proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). Furthermore, the objection that the causal consideration (*kāraṇībhūtaparāmarśa*) consists in the apprehension of the pervasion of the locus of both [existence and non-existence] through identity with that [relation], and the apprehension of the pervasiveness of the absence of the reason, is refuted. This is because the inferential process cannot be prevented prior to its occurrence by the people’s cognition in the form of a mutual negation—characterized as a contradiction between existence and non-existence—and because [the object] is grasped as possessing non-existence conditioned by the absence of existence.

This is incorrect because, when shell-silver and the like are apprehended as being identical with that [silver] by virtue of being the locus of both [its appearance and its non-existence], the cognition negating pervasion—arising from the apprehension of the reason (the property of being sublated) within the example—is unavoidable even prior to the formal division of the argument into the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth; thus, the absence of the reason [in the subject] is already established.

This is the method of analysis (*ūha*). Here, if the object established as "existent" (*sat*) is qualified by non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*), then its identity (*tādātmya*) would be nothing other than identity with non-sublatability. In that case, even while [the object] is sublatable, it would be said to possess non-sublatability; and thus, how could there not be a self-contradiction (*svavyāhati*)? If, on the other hand, it is "existent" because it is the object of the cognition "it exists," then its identity would be the state of being cognized as existent. In that case, it would be a different matter (*arthāntara*), because even the proponent of the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti-vādin*) accepts that things such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell are objects of the cognition "it exists."

Now, suppose it is argued: "Identity (*tādātmya*) is a specific type of relation. Thus, identity with the non-sublatable (*abādhyatādātmya*) is not identical to the nature of being non-sublatable; so how can there be a contradiction? If this is said, we reply: No. For such a relation—just as the identity that exists between a blue thing and a pot—is possible in some other form, distinct from that [specific] identity yet denotable by the word "that" (*tat*), provided it is the object of an error whose locus is the non-sublatable. This is because [such a relation] could exist even while being a relation such as being the object of a cognition that is removable by a certain knowledge (namely, the knowledge of the non-sublatable).

It is impossible for there to be an exclusion of the non-existent (*asad-vyāvṛtti*) by the mere fact of being its means of proof. Since its identity and genus are well-established, and since those depend upon difference and non-difference, it follows that there is also non-difference with that which is non-sublated; how then could there be sublation in the form of absolute difference delimited by non-sublation? Otherwise, just as there is the cognition "the pot is blue," there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cognition "the sublatable is the non-sublatable."

Because the apprehension of absolute difference from that which is delimited by a particular property (*taddharmāvacchinna*) is precisely what constitutes an opposition to the apprehension of identity with that same property-delimited object; thus, for that which exists as an uncontradicted identity, its state of being contradicted cannot take the form of an absolute difference from the uncontradicted. Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction because the difference from the uncontradicted possesses a higher degree of reality (*adhikasattāka*) than the identity; for until the establishment of indeterminacy (*anirvacanīyatva*) through inference for oneself (*svārthānumiti*), the aforementioned difference possessing [a specific] reality does not present itself, and therefore the pacification of the contradiction is impossible.
Furthermore, since it must be stated that in the world both the aforementioned difference and identity possess only a conventional (vyāvahārika) status, a contradiction cannot be resolved.

Nor should it be argued that the identity with the mother-of-pearl in the silver does not have non-sublatability as its delimiting property of counter-correlativity, but rather has "thisness" (idantva) and so forth as its delimiting property; for since there exists sublatibility in the form of absolute difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by non-sublatability, the linguistic usage "the unsublatable is sublatable" would result [absurdly]. Nor should it be argued that even in the definition of indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva), no fault arises because identity is introduced as being determined by the locus of non-sublatability.

For, in whatever form [an object] exists as absolutely distinct from something else, it is contradicted by all experience that there could be either difference-cum-identity or identity dependent upon that [other] with respect to it in some other form. Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the knowledge arising from the sentence "Water is drinkable," which contains the word "water" intending [to refer to] ice and so forth, would be valid; because according to your own view, even though there is absolute difference between [the water] as ice and as something drinkable, there is no sublation of its identity with that which is delimited by the property of waterhood (*jalatva*).

And you yourself, on the occasion of commenting on the *Vācaspatikārikās*, stated: "There is no identity even through [the common property of] being gold between a bracelet and an earring that exist at different places and times simultaneously. Nor should it be argued that while there is no identity through [the common property of] being gold between a bracelet and an earring derived from the same single instance of gold, their absolute difference as a bracelet and as an earring was also stated in that very same place; for it is simply untenable to claim that there is no identity in any form whatsoever for that which is absolutely different in any form whatsoever.

Even in that case, because there is no cognition such as "this earring is non-different from that bracelet by virtue of being gold," non-difference with that earring as the counter-correlate is not admitted for that bracelet even in the form of "gold-ness"; for non-difference is admitted only in relation to the substrate of gold-ness residing in its material cause (*upādāna*). For this very reason, it was stated in that same work: "The distinct determination of color, taste, and so forth, residing in a single jar that is absolutely different [from other jars], is exactly like this."

Nor should it be argued that there can be identity between the silver, which has existence as its material cause (*sadupādānaka*), and existence itself; for since [the silver] is perceived as absolutely distinct from it, it is impossible for it to have existence as its material cause—just as a cloth, which is perceived as absolutely distinct from clay, is not seen to have clay as its material cause—and because such identity would lack a locus of non-sublation in the case of the silver.

Furthermore, since sublatedness (*bādhyatva*) itself has been made the reason (*hetu*), when proving identity with existence qualified by sublatedness (*bādhyatvaviśiṣṭasattādātmya*), the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*) serves no significant purpose within the body of the probandum (*sādhya*). Moreover, if the probandum were the qualified entity, there would be a contradiction for the reason of sublatedness in either proving identity with existence in the form of non-sublated identity by discarding the qualification, or in proving identity with existence as such. Nor is it correct to say that existence is simply the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and that what is being proved is identity delimited by that [capacity].

Because there is both sublation (*bādha*) and contradiction in attempting to establish identity with that [sublated object] which is already understood as being distinct from that which performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*); and because the Buddhist proponent of the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti-vādin*) accepts that even the sublated object possesses causal efficiency, so that if he were to admit that this very [efficiency] constitutes its "indefinability" (*anirvacanīyatva*) in the world, his distinction from the Buddhist would not be established. Therefore, in order to establish that [distinction], another kind of indefinability must be defined for the world; and since such [another kind] must be stated regarding the examples (such as nacre-silver) used in the inference proving it, [the original argument fails].

Nor can any cognition in the form “all that exists is knowable” constitute identity with its respective objects; for if that [identity] were to be established by means of the cognition itself, then since that cognition would be recognized simply as a cognition, it would also include the recognition of an error such as “all exists” which has nacre-silver and the like as its object. Consequently, even on the view that nacre-silver and so forth are non-existent, the identity with those objects—which are the content of that error—would still exist [within the cognition], and thus the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) cannot be avoided.

Because it is impossible to determine among cognitions of such a form whether "this is indeed valid knowledge" or "this is indeed an error," it is impossible to specify and include any particular individual instance. Furthermore, if one were to identify [the object] as being an error of that form, then since its objective status (*viṣayatā*) is admitted in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*); nor is there any such particular instance of valid knowledge whose identification as such [an error] could be made.

Just as it is impossible to deny the universal, constant, and world-renowned fact that when a thing is apprehended as being absolutely distinct from a jar, there is an apprehension of its absolute difference from the object of a valid cognition (pramā) whose qualifier is "jar-ness"—an apprehension which is compelled by reason—so too here, when silver is apprehended as being absolutely distinct from existence in the form "the silver is indeed non-existent," it is impossible to deny the apprehension of its absolute difference from the object of a valid cognition whose qualifier is "existence," and specifically the apprehension of its absolute difference from the particular instance of such a valid cognition.

For, in establishing the identity of such silver with the object of such a valid cognition (*pramā*), it is impossible to avoid both the sublation (*bādha*) by the reason of being sublated and the lack of contradiction (*avirodha*). Otherwise, there would follow the absurdity that even in a jar—which is distinct from the object of the valid cognition "it is blue," or which is ascertained to possess absolute difference from the specific object of the valid cognition "all is blue"—the identity with blueness could be established. Nor should it be argued that this contradiction is not accepted by the proponents of the theory of the indescribable (*anirvacanīya-vādin*).

Because the aforementioned contradiction, which is established by all the world, cannot be set aside by mere whim due to the perception of the indeterminable (anirvacanīya), it has already been stated that even inference for oneself (svārthānumiti) is impossible.

However, the aforementioned method does not cohere in any way with respect to inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). If that particular instance is accepted by both [parties] as having silver as its object in the form of the cognition "this is silver," then it is precisely the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of such an instance that is unacceptable to me; thus, it is improper to present it to me. If, on the other hand, a cognition established in both systems is taken as one that does not have that [silver] as its object, then there is simply a contradiction (*bādha*).

If a cognition that is accepted by the neutral observer and the opponent as not having silver or the like as its object, yet is accepted solely on the basis of one's own view as having that as its object, is then taken up, an inference of identity with that [silver] cannot possibly occur for either the neutral observer or the proponent, since it is being apprehended as absolutely distinct from its object.

Furthermore, if the cognition "all that is knowable is real" (sarvaṃ satprameyam)—which is accepted as valid knowledge (*pramā*) and as having silver-in-ivory as its object—is admitted under both views, then the acceptance of that specific instance as valid knowledge cannot be established without accepting the reality of the silver-in-ivory; thus, it should be understood that the proof of identity with Being (*sattādātmya*) in that case would be entirely redundant.

Furthermore, if the meaning of "valid cognition having the form 'existent'" (*sad-ity-ākāraka-pramā*) is "valid cognition expressible by a sentence containing the word 'existent'," then—since it is possible to cognize even a non-existent thing through the word 'existent' by means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as in the case of the error regarding mother-of-pearl, or by means of a modern convention (*ādhunika-saṅketa*)—the attempt to establish identity with that [cognition] as its object would result in nothing but the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*).

If it is argued that the valid cognition (*pramā*) produced by such a sentence is independent of errors regarding mother-of-pearl and the like, then there arises the unwanted consequence (*āpatti*) that the sentence "everything that is knowable is real" would also include the valid cognition whose qualifier is "correctness" (*samīcīnatva*), even though this cognition occurs without any error concerning mother-of-pearl. Consequently, one could not avoid the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*) when attempting to establish identity with the object of that [sentence]. For it is not the case that there is no linguistic convention (*śakti*) for "correctness" and so forth as established in the lexicons; rather, there is a royal decree that the term applies to that which is delimited by non-sublatedness (*abādhyatva*).

If that [cognition] is included by way of being a valid cognition whose content is the qualifier "non-sublated," then since it is possible to include it by way of being a valid cognition whose content is the qualifier "non-sublated," there would be the fallacy of "wrapping one's head" (unnecessary complication). If, on the other hand, that [qualification] is omitted and it is included in that same manner, then when proving the identity with the object of that particular instance of valid cognition which is ascertained as being different from the non-sublatable, there is precisely the aforementioned sublation and so forth.

If it is argued that the probandum is identity with the universal of existence (*sattājāti*), we say no. For even when silver is perceived as identical with substance-ness (*dravyatva*), silver-ness (*rajatatva*), and so forth, there is a cessation of doubts such as its non-existence or its having a non-existent substrate; yet in that [opponent's] view, such doubts would not cease through the knowledge of identity with the aforementioned existence. Since the two cases are equal, this fails to avoid the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*).

If the cognition of identity with substance (*dravyatādātmyajñāna*) were also a remover of that [doubt], then—since such a doubt would have been either removed or prevented from arising by the force of cognitions established through common usage (*vyavahāra*) and other means, such as "silver is a substance"—the proof of identity with Being (*sattādātmya*) would result in being entirely ineffective. Furthermore, there is no determining factor for why the cognition of identity with substance does not oppose the aforementioned doubt, while the cognition of identity with Being alone does.
Finally, since the universal of Being (*sattājāti*), like the universals of substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so forth, is grasped by perception, it is improper to attempt to prove identity with it.

By this, the following is refuted: [the claim] that in the cognition having the form "existent" (sat), the identity delimited by that which is the mode (*prakāra*) in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) is what is established as the probandum (*sādhya*), whereas properties such as "correctness" (*samīcīnatva*) and so forth are not so. For if such a property were existence (*sattā*), there would be the fallacy of proving the already established (*arthāntara*); if it were non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*), there would be the very fallacy of contradiction (*bādha*), and thus the aforementioned defects cannot be avoided. Furthermore, identity connected with time is also refuted by the same reasons of *arthāntara*, contradiction, and so on.

Or, let there be some kind of identity with existence (*sattādātmya*) established by the cognition "this is existent. You must state the utility of proving that [identity]. If you say it is for the purpose of refuting the Buddhist doctrine of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), we say no; for since even in the case of something non-existent like a rabbit's horn, identity with existence is unavoidable by the force of the cognition "the rabbit's horn is existent," that [identity] cannot serve to exclude its non-existence.

The specific qualification—"the identity with indefinable existence does not exist in the non-existent"—is established as follows: the cause for the conventional usage of "rabbit's horn" and the like is mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), whereas the cause for the conventional usage of "silver in a mother-of-pearl shell" and the like is cognition (*jñāna*). Therefore, it is precisely the identity with existence established by such apprehension that is introduced; thus, the statement "thereby there is exclusion of the non-existent" [is made]. Furthermore, in the apprehension "the rabbit's horn exists," it is only a relation to time that is perceived.

However, the specific statement that "it does not possess identity with existence (*sattādātmya*)," the claim that "in the cognition 'the horn of a rabbit exists,' only the indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) is perceived, whereas non-existence (*asat*) is entirely devoid of designation; therefore, it does not possess identity with existence," and the assertion that "from the sentence 'the horn of a rabbit,' only a cognition with a discordant qualifier arises"—such ill-spoken remarks will be refuted in the section concerning the rejection of *arthāpatti* and other means of proof.
Thus ends the *Dvaitadyumaṇipariśiṣṭa*.
